data.title: Selling cryptocurrency to pay off debts and betting on AI: Mining companies are facing a double whammy.
data.description:
Author: Zhou, ChainCatcher

Since November, Bitcoin has fallen by more than 20%, once approaching $55,000, hitting a new low since September 2024.

Mining revenue has shrunk accordingly. According to Antpool data, based on an electricity price of $0.06 per kilowatt-hour, electricity costs for newer models such as the Antminer T21 and Whatsminer M60S series account for more than 97% of revenue, basically only breaking even. The Avalon A1466I has even fallen below its shutdown price.

Over the past year, listed mining companies have adopted almost identical strategies to cope with the bear market: selling off their Bitcoin holdings while transferring electricity and facilities to AI companies. The consensus in the market was that mining companies were withdrawing en masse and turning to AI, which was more profitable.

However, in November, the AI ​​sector also experienced significant volatility. In the two weeks following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation and subsequent reinstatement, the stock prices of mining companies that transitioned to AI also fluctuated wildly. This means that the AI ​​business that mining companies originally used to hedge against cryptocurrency prices is becoming a new source of risk.

I. Mining rigs are still running, but mining is no longer profitable

According to Hashrate Index data, as of November 25th, the Bitcoin hashrate price fell to $27.74 per PH per day, a near one-year low. However, the 7-day average hashrate of the entire network is still 1048.8 EH/s, and there has been no large-scale shutdown of mining rigs. Hashrate Index predicts that the difficulty adjustment on November 27th will increase by approximately 8.6%.

Regarding miner revenue, according to Newhedge data, total miner revenue in October was approximately $1.215 billion, the highest in 11 months; entering November, revenue so far is only about $740 million, and at this rate, total revenue for the month will be significantly lower than October's.

The cost pressure on listed mining companies has already become apparent. CoinShares' Q2 mining report shows that the weighted average cash cost for listed mining companies to mine one Bitcoin was approximately $75,500, while the Bitcoin price at the end of the quarter was only $58,400, causing the industry as a whole to fall below the cash break-even point.

The price of Bitcoin has now returned to this level. Twenty One Capital CEO Rapha Zagury previously stated that Bitcoin is experiencing its first-ever hashrate bear market, with fewer and fewer listed mining companies able to continue large-scale mining. II. Who is selling Bitcoin? Mining is not profitable, so mining companies are starting to sell their coins. According to Lookonchain statistics, as of November 10th, 14 listed companies have sold a total of 108,247 Bitcoins this year, worth approximately $8.08 billion, the vast majority of which were sold by mining companies. MARA and Riot sold 40,581 and 20,264 Bitcoins respectively, accounting for more than half of the total. Glassnode also points out that while listed mining companies have held onto their mined Bitcoins for years, and even bought some additional ones, they have sold nearly half of their reserves since January of this year. These Bitcoins are now being used to fund the transformation of AI data centers. Their charts show a net decrease of approximately 27,000 Bitcoins in November alone, the largest drop on record. On another note, even when selling Bitcoins, the purposes differ from company to company. MARA disclosed in its Q3 shareholder letter that it sold 13,597 Bitcoins at an average price of approximately $81,039 at the end of the quarter, raising approximately $1.1 billion, of which $750 million was used to pay off Bitcoin mortgage loans. Previously, MARA had sold cryptocurrency to repurchase approximately $1 billion in convertible bonds, reducing its debt by $1.4 billion in the first three quarters, a 37% decrease. This means MARA's cryptocurrency sales were primarily to repay the leverage left over from its previous expansion. Riot, on the other hand, invested the proceeds from its cryptocurrency sales in data centers. According to its Q3 financial report, Riot sold 20,264 Bitcoins in the first three quarters of this year, raising approximately $1.5 billion, mainly for data center construction. It did not conduct any equity financing throughout the year. III. Betting on AI: Where Did the Money from Cryptocurrency Sales Go? Mining companies' bets on AI have a very direct calculation behind them. CoinShares estimates that each megawatt of AI computing power can bring in approximately $1.5 million in profit annually, while Bitcoin mining only generates about $500,000. The capital market is also willing to pay a premium for this. Benoît Pellevoizin, Managing Director of CoinShares France, stated that mining companies that have signed contracts for AI capacity are trading at an average of 12.9 times their forward sales, while those without contracts are only trading at 3.7 times. The transformation narrative reached its peak in September when Grayscale renamed its Bitcoin Mining ETF to the AI ​​Hashrate ETF, changing its ticker symbol from MNRS to GCPU, and switching its tracking index to the Indxx High Performance Computing Index. However, the other side of this equation is the enormous investment required. CoinShares estimates that converting a mining farm into AI infrastructure costs between $8 million and $15 million per megawatt, more than ten times the cost of building a mining farm. According to BlocksBridge Consulting, the capital expenditures of nine listed mining companies reached $5.11 billion in the first half of this year, while AI and high-performance computing revenue was only $341 million during the same period, meaning the investment was 15 times the revenue. From a transformation perspective, mining companies can be broadly categorized into three types. The first type consists of landlords with long-term leases, represented by Riot, TeraWulf, and Cipher. Riot leased its entire Corsicana campus for 15 years, a contract valued at approximately $28 billion, with its 10-Q filing showing Anthropic as the tenant. TeraWulf signed a 20-year lease with Anthropic, worth approximately $19 billion. It's also worth noting that most of these leases won't commence until the second half of 2027, and the long-term revenue of several mining companies is tied to the same AI company. The second type comprises self-operated computing power providers, represented by IREN. IREN procures its own GPUs and provides computing power services to clients like Microsoft, offering greater revenue flexibility but also bearing the risks of GPU depreciation and customer concentration. The third category consists of mining companies whose transformation has not yet been implemented, a typical example being MARA. It sold the most cryptocurrencies this year, but its shareholder letter shows that it has not signed a single data center lease to date, and the only signed AI contract is a four-year, $79 million GPU service contract with its subsidiary Exaion. In November, when AI stocks experienced increased volatility, MARA reiterated in its shareholder letter that Bitcoin mining remains the company's core business. **[Image of image: https://img.jinse.com.cn/7524523]** **IV. Two-Way Failure: The Market Begins to Categorize Mining Companies** **The sharp fluctuations in the AI ​​sector in November disrupted this path.** According to a Bloomberg report on November 5th, Microsoft tightened its oversight of neocloud projects such as Nebius, IREN, and Nscale, withdrawing from projects it deemed risky and internally discussing whether to continue signing new neocloud contracts. On the same day, IREN, in its earnings report, postponed its annualized revenue target of over $4 billion from the end of 2026 to January 2027, stating that it might be delayed until February due to design changes requested by customers and supplier schedules. Subsequently, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on November 12th but was reinstated by the board on the 23rd. The stock price of the company, which had transitioned to mining, subsequently fluctuated wildly. Based on Nasdaq closing prices, from November 13th to 20th, IREN fell 34.9% in a week, MARA fell 27.2%, and Bitcoin fell approximately 15% during the same period. On the day Huang Renxun returned to office, mining stocks rebounded collectively, with IREN surging over 20%, before falling back 11.54% the following day. From the price trends, these companies' stock prices have increasingly followed AI sentiment, with Bitcoin taking a secondary role. A deeper problem lies in financing. The Bitcoin buffer has been sold, and most AI leases won't start until after 2027. During this period, construction funds can only rely on external financing. Unfortunately, the financing environment is tightening. IREN disclosed that approximately $6 billion in financing for the remaining capital expenditures in fiscal year 2027 remains unsecured, depending on market conditions. Cipher has agreed to assume the first $359.3 million over budget for the Barber Lake project. Riot management mentioned in the Q3 conference call that rising interest rates and widening credit spreads have led lenders to significantly tighten their scrutiny of tenants' credit, power supply, and delivery records. Project financing for the Corsicana project will not begin until 2027. If loans cannot be secured under market conditions, tenants will advance approximately $3.6 billion in construction costs, which will then be deducted from rent at an implied annual interest rate of approximately 12%. The market has also begun to reprice mining companies accordingly. As of the closing bell on November 24th, Riot was up 25.6% year-to-date, while IREN and Cipher were down 66.8% and 63.1% respectively, MARA was down 41.1%, TeraWulf was down 14.5%, and Bitcoin was down 31.5% year-to-date.

Riot, which has secured top tenants and doesn't currently need equity financing, is one of the few exceptions. IREN, which has purchased its own GPUs and still has a financing gap, saw the deepest decline.

Of course, based on publicly disclosed information, no signed leases have been cancelled yet. Mining companies are currently facing pressure from valuation, financing, and delivery.

V. Epilogue

Overall, it's difficult for mining companies to return to their original path. According to Hashrate Index estimates, the next halving will occur around April 2028, at which time the block reward will be halved again. CoinShares analyst Luke Nolan also believes that even if the price of Bitcoin recovers, it will be difficult to reverse the transformation of mining companies towards AI.

This also raises a bigger question. Listed mining companies were once the main force of Bitcoin's hash power; now that they are gradually transferring electricity and facilities to AI companies, who will take over the hash power they leave behind?

In May of this year, VanEck proposed that as US-listed mining companies shift their electricity to AI hyperscale customers, idle hydroelectric and natural gas resources controlled by governments will naturally succeed Bitcoin mining. If this assessment holds true, the security budget for the Bitcoin network will increasingly be borne by sovereign entities and low-cost energy providers, while Wall Street-backed listed mining companies will gradually become the electricity landlords of the AI ​​era. For Bitcoin, this may signify another shift in the computing power landscape, with a more decentralized and unpredictable group of participants taking over.

data.title: Interview with BitMEX Founder: AI Giants Will Eventually Be Nationalized; Betting on Bitcoin
data.description:
Author: The Defiant; Translator: Plain Language Blockchain

Why does Arthur Hayes, co-founder of BitMEX, who predicted Bitcoin would reach $250,000 at the beginning of the year, admit to misjudging the market this year?

In a recent interview with Unchained, he made a market-shaking prediction: the artificial intelligence bubble has not yet burst, but once it does, it will force central banks around the world to launch an epic money-printing bailout—and this is the only engine for Bitcoin to repeat its explosive bull run.

In addition, he also sharply predicted the fate of giants like OpenAI heading towards "nationalization," revealed for the first time the decentralized payment network Flop, which was built specifically for AI agents, and directly named the three core betting targets under next year's massive bailout scenario.

Sharp insights, packed with valuable information, let's explore the truth! I. Reviewing the Logic Behind Bitcoin Predictions and the Bursting of the AI ​​Bubble Host: Welcome to the Unchained podcast. Our guest today is Arthur Hayes, co-founder of BitMEX. Arthur, welcome back to our show. Arthur Hayes: Thank you for the invitation. Host: Listeners are very familiar with Arthur's achievements. He co-founded BitMEX and invented the most popular perpetual swap contract in the cryptocurrency space. Currently, he oversees investments at his family office, Maelstrom, and also writes a widely followed macroeconomic newsletter. In addition, he has returned to the forefront from semi-retirement, founding and operating Flop Labs since August of this year. Its experimental testnet will officially launch on November 24th (the day after this program's recording). This year, you've publicly reversed your positions on market predictions several times. In May, you referred to Hyperliquid, NEAR, and Zcash as the "Holy Trinity," but later abandoned these expectations; last Monday, you referred to Ethereum (ETH), Zcash, NEAR, and Ethena as the "Four Horsemen," but subsequently announced that all four positions had been closed. Meanwhile, you set a target price of $250,000 for Bitcoin at the beginning of the year, which now seems unlikely to be achieved unless there is a significant market movement in the next month and a half. Let's start with Bitcoin. You set a target of $250,000 in March, lowered your expectations in April, and now Bitcoin is around $62,000. Where do you think your core logic went wrong this year? Arthur Hayes: Ultimately, the reason is that not enough money has been printed. The market had expected further monetary easing, but that didn't happen, hence Bitcoin's weakness. It's now clear that we're facing various headwinds related to artificial intelligence (AI), and the market is starting to question whether AI investment is a huge waste of money, which is why Bitcoin hasn't benefited. That's where I misjudged things this year. Host: Next, let's talk about your views on artificial intelligence, which is very interesting. You believe there's an AI bubble currently, and its bursting will force the Federal Reserve to adopt a more accommodative monetary policy. Can you explain the logic behind this in detail? Arthur Hayes: In short, if you look at the most advanced and well-funded AI labs right now—Anthropic and OpenAI—neither of them are profitable; in fact, they're losing huge sums of money. Even if you examine Anthropic's S-1 prospectus, you won't see any hope of achieving profitability in the near future. They are continuously expanding their spending, pouring funds into massive capital expenditures, whether building data centers or developing their own chips, and they have also signed numerous non-cancellable computing power procurement contracts. I am 100% convinced that artificial intelligence will have a highly transformative impact on human civilization. However, given the current investment opportunities and the underlying logic supporting the current AI and computing center bull market, these two leading companies in the world are not making money at all; on the contrary, they are incurring huge losses. This is essentially a story of credit expansion. Everyone believes in the transformative power of AI, so massive amounts of credit have flooded into the industry. Governments in the United States and around the world are also supporting this process because data center construction brings tax revenue, and rising stock markets create a wealth effect and increase consumption—positive externalities generated during an investment bubble. Thus, credit continues to flow. But now, people are beginning to question: will these investments bring substantial returns in the future? Are Anthropic and OpenAI capable of fulfilling their obligations to purchase hundreds of billions of dollars worth of computing power in 2027, 2028, 2029, and beyond? If they cannot, or if the market begins to question the solvency of these credit lines, then building these data centers loses its commercial viability. The seriousness of the problem lies in the fact that many participants have expanded their credit through highly leveraged borrowing. I believe that starting in the second half of 2027, these issues will truly confront investors and could trigger a massive market crash.

Host: The market has recently experienced some sharp fluctuations, with the Nasdaq index experiencing a significant correction. On the very day we recorded this program, Jensen Huang had just returned, Nvidia's stock price surged 30% in a single day, and the Nasdaq index also rose 6%. What are your thoughts on these signals?

Arthur Hayes: This is precisely a warning sign, foreshadowing what is to come. I don't believe the AI ​​bubble has burst yet; it hasn't truly exploded. However, when it does, it will inevitably trigger a broad-based easing of monetary policy. Unfortunately, cryptocurrencies are considered highly liquid assets in people's asset allocations, so when investors are forced to sell AI stocks, they will also sell cryptocurrencies simultaneously, causing Bitcoin's price to fall. But if you can construct your portfolio reasonably, use leverage prudently or even avoid it altogether, and control your position size to match your capital, then when central banks start printing money again, you will have the opportunity to obtain huge returns on Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies similar to those in 2008 and 2020. In fact, we have already seen the reaction mechanisms of various governments. Taiwan and South Korea have introduced market rescue measures to support their stock markets, allowing retail traders to use higher leverage, using government investment funds to buy stocks in the open market, and prohibiting short selling. This shows that these markets have been more severely impacted than the US market, which is an early sign of the future evolution of the AI ​​industry. We've even seen US President Donald Trump personally intervene in a private company's board decision to reinstate Jensen Huang, as previous changes had dampened market sentiment. Weakening the power of the CEO, dubbed the "central bank of artificial intelligence," would raise doubts about Nvidia's ability to fulfill its computing power delivery obligations to AI labs and cloud service providers. Therefore, they were forced to recall Huang overnight because they needed the stock price to rise and market confidence to be boosted. This clearly demonstrates that the whole world is betting on the same thing: everyone is counting on AI to continue rising, and every economy is highly dependent on the AI ​​supply chain. If AI falters, the whole world will fall into recession, so all leaders will do everything in their power to prop up the market. The signs of a bailout mechanism are already emerging. I'm not sure if the Federal Reserve will shift to easing at its December meeting in a few weeks based on the recent market turmoil, but we know that massive quantitative easing is inevitable. Even the US president is willing to personally intervene in private companies, recalling a CEO who was accused of having ties to China—regardless of the veracity of the accusations, this is politically extremely sensitive and a minefield. However, the US president is clearly more concerned with the rise of the Nasdaq index than with national security agencies' concerns about chip export compliance. This sufficiently demonstrates the importance of AI transactions to the government, and should also be a reassurance to cryptocurrency investors: in the medium term, we will definitely see a large-scale bailout plan. Maybe not now, maybe it will take 18 months, but it will eventually come, and it will be enormous. Host: You mean whether the Bitcoin market can rebound significantly after its current slump depends entirely on whether this bailout plan is implemented? Arthur Hayes: Absolutely. In my view, besides printing money, Bitcoin has no other price-driving engine. It is essentially a transaction based on the devaluation of fiat currency. As long as the global supply of US dollars or fiat currency increases significantly, and assuming the technology itself remains effective, the price of Bitcoin will mathematically and inevitably rise. I believe this technology, proven reliable over 15 years, is entirely reliable. Of course, some may mention the risks of quantum computing, but concerns about quantum computing have existed since I entered the crypto industry, and I don't think it will be a fatal problem in the future. The entire logic concerns only the speed of money creation or destruction, which is the only factor determining the price of Bitcoin. If we want to see a super bull market like in 2020, we need massive money printing, and this will only happen when the AI ​​bubble bursts.

II. Tightening or Printing Money? Trading Timing and Predictive Methodology

Host: Assuming your judgment is correct, artificial intelligence is indeed a bubble that will eventually burst, but what if the US government doesn't intervene? Is the continued rise in US debt levels sufficient to support the logic of Bitcoin's devaluation? Arthur Hayes: If they hadn't bailed out the artificial intelligence industry—the largest investment boom in human history since the railroad era—the world would have experienced a Great Depression worse than that of 1929. What happened in the early 1930s? The stock market crashed, and gold prices plummeted because the U.S. and many other countries initially decided not to intervene, refusing to provide sufficient credit, embracing free-market capitalism and allowing over-leveraged companies to go bankrupt. It was a severe credit crunch. In that environment, while gold or hard assets would outperform all other financial assets, your nominal wealth would still shrink significantly. However, I think this scenario is highly unlikely today. By contrast, expecting governments to implement austerity measures is an unrealistic fantasy. Austerity is politically unpopular; Herbert Hoover served only one term as U.S. president and was branded with the stigma of the Great Depression precisely because of his attempts to implement austerity. While in the long run, the prolonged austerity cleared out bad credit, allowing the US to restore low inflation and a healthier fiscal budget than European powers before World War II—short-term pain for long-term health—in modern political systems, whether it's a government like China or a representative republic like the US, voters and the public don't want fiscal austerity; they demand the government print money. When markets crash and all ships are sinking, the government gains overwhelming political cover, allowing it to disregard concerns about inflation, fiscal discipline, and the independence of the Federal Reserve, and directly start printing money. I predict the real bursting of the AI ​​bubble will begin in the second half of 2027. The specific trigger point depends on the speed of the collapse, who goes bankrupt, and their political influence.

Host: Back to the present, the Federal Reserve is about to hold its interest rate meeting in December. What do you expect to happen next? Arthur Hayes: Based on the current discussions and recent statements from Federal Reserve official Williams, the US economy still faces inflationary pressures. Some officials believe it's necessary to maintain a tightening or interest rate hike stance, the key being whether an internal consensus can be reached. As a cryptocurrency investor, I at least hope to see the Fed stop raising interest rates and restart "reserve management purchases" (which is essentially another way of saying quantitative easing). To me, this would be a clear signal that they don't want to see the market overreact before intervention, which would be an excellent opportunity to increase cryptocurrency exposure, as Bitcoin may have already hit a temporary bottom around $55,000, and other altcoins have fallen even further. A very healthy rebound would follow from these lows. However, I'm not yet sure if the Fed has changed its stance; we need to continue observing the December meeting statement. Host: What would happen to the market if the Fed reached a hawkish consensus and raised interest rates by 25 basis points? Arthur Hayes: The market will fall sharply due to soaring financing costs. The market is already questioning the debt levels and financing costs of AI companies, especially emerging cloud computing companies like CoreWeave. If the federal funds rate stays around 4.25%, investors can get over 4% returns with zero risk simply by buying US Treasury bonds, outperforming inflation. Why risk default by buying bonds of loss-making AI companies? Look at Anthropic's initial public offering (IPO); the share price was only slightly above the offering range. The market initially expected Nvidia's 30% surge to boost Anthropic, but it opened high and then plummeted, performing very poorly. These companies are unprofitable yet require unlimited funds to maintain capital expenditures, making them a "poison pill" for secondary market investors. Worse still, Anthropic has the ability to issue new shares on the public market (ATM) at any time to pay off its debts, and many employees, having become incredibly wealthy on paper, need to cash out to buy mansions, luxury watches, and high-end cars. Under immense selling pressure, the only possible direction for the stock price is downward.

Host: Why can't top labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, with their revolutionary technologies, simply raise product prices to achieve profitability?

Arthur Hayes: If they were the sole monopolist in the market, they could certainly do so, but the reality is that market competition is extremely fierce. Moreover, 99% of ordinary users and businesses don't need to fold proteins or solve the Riemann Hypothesis. The vast majority of people simply need an AI agent to help with bank applications, restaurant reservations, itinerary planning, or email summaries. We don't need the most expensive cutting-edge models; we just need models that are "good enough and cheap." Currently, open-source models have emerged in China, achieving 95% of the performance of top-tier closed-source models in most tests, but at only 1% of the cost. More importantly, companies can deploy open-source models on their own private servers or local data centers, maintaining complete control over data flow and access permissions, without having to hand over their core trade secrets to the "black boxes" of Silicon Valley tech giants. Neither consumers nor businesses have any reason to pay a premium for closed-source models unless dealing with extremely challenging research tasks. Therefore, these labs simply cannot generate enough revenue to support a valuation of trillions of dollars. Host: What will happen if they cannot achieve commercial profitability? Arthur Hayes: They will eventually be bailed out by the government and evolve into entities similar to defense contractors or public utility companies. The U.S. Department of Defense will allocate hundreds of billions, even trillions, of its AI budget to OpenAI and Anthropic. They won't become super growth stocks with a market capitalization of $2 trillion, but rather "waterworks" strictly regulated by the government—the government decides your profit margins, employee structure, product form, and target customers. During a market frenzy, I would never buy a "waterworks" valued at $1.5 trillion; but if it crashes by more than 50% and its valuation returns to around $200 billion, I might consider allocating some funds. As for the real winners in AI application layers that will bring high growth in the future, I think they haven't even emerged yet, just as you couldn't foresee Facebook, Alibaba, ByteDance, or Tencent during the dot-com bubble of 2000.

Host: Talk about the "Four Horsemen" (ETH, Zcash, NEAR, and Ethena) you closed out last week. Why didn't this trade go as expected?

Arthur Hayes: I originally bet that Anthropic's IPO would be a huge success, reigniting market enthusiasm for the AI ​​narrative. Therefore, I chose NEAR and Venice (AI concept tokens) as high-elasticity assets, while also allocating to Zcash and ETH, which have better liquidity. I expected these high-beta assets to outperform Bitcoin in a context of rising risk appetite and looser credit. However, Anthropic opened high and closed low after its IPO, and related tokens followed suit. I realized I had misjudged the situation, and since my position was already small, I decisively cut my losses and exited the market. As for Zcash, my initial position was large, but as the price rose, my attention to it decreased because I couldn't control its technological development. Now I've re-established a position in Zcash, but purely as a "high-beta version of Bitcoin." It inherits Bitcoin's core attributes while carrying a privacy narrative, resulting in extremely high volatility—if Bitcoin rises by 10%, Zcash could potentially double. I no longer worry about whether its privacy technology is perfect; I'm now trading based entirely on price levels and market narratives. Host: As a medium- to long-term investor, how would you determine the timing for a major re-entry into Bitcoin and Zcash? Arthur Hayes: In the next round of reflation triggered by central bank bailouts, I would closely watch two signals: First, gold outperforming the Nasdaq. Looking back at last summer's market, before the Fed intervened in the yen and initiated Treasury bond buybacks, gold peaked days to weeks earlier than Bitcoin, followed by Bitcoin, and finally the Nasdaq; and in the subsequent decline, gold was also the first to correct. Therefore, if I see the stock market consolidating or declining while gold begins to strengthen independently, it means that macro liquidity expectations are shifting, and I will begin to build positions in stages. Second, dovish statements from Federal Reserve Board (FOMC) voting members. If previously hawkish officials begin hinting at restarting asset purchases or resuming reserve management, it would repeat the history of Powell's major policy shift in December 2018—when the S&P 500 plummeted by about 20% at the end of the year, and Powell subsequently shifted to easing, initiating a steady rise that lasted for more than a year.

Host: You often receive criticism on social media—for example, SageXPT accuses you of publicly recommending stocks to dump your holdings on your followers. How do you respond to such criticism?

Arthur Hayes: First of all, I am not a financial advisor, nor have I ever managed any external clients' funds; I only manage my own money. I publish articles and predictions publicly to test my investment logic. If I cannot put my views in the public sphere for scrutiny and criticism, I have no reason to risk my hard-earned money. If you blindly follow anyone's advice online and lose money, that is your own responsibility because you did not think independently. My investment principle is "Strong convictions, loosely held." I might change my mind in the next minute. I publicly express my views to see external feedback, especially the private opinions of several senior hedge fund trader friends I respect—they are very intelligent, often disagree with me, and through debate, I can discover blind spots in my logic. As for the noise on social media, I don't care at all. The best traders aren't always right; they're wrong most of the time, but the key is that they know why they enter a market, when to admit their mistakes and exit, and to go all in on truly high-certainty opportunities. III. Betting on the AI ​​Agent Economy: Why Found Flop Network? Host: Next, let's talk about your new project, Flop Network. The testnet is launching tomorrow. What is the core concept of this project? What are your expectations for its launch? Arthur Hayes: Simply put, I want to create a payment network specifically for the AI ​​agentic economy. While I predict a bubble in AI infrastructure, every investment bubble ultimately leaves a valuable legacy for the next era. Overinvestment in data centers will generate enormous and extremely cheap computing power. Economic laws tell us that when a good becomes extremely cheap, its consumption grows exponentially. In computer science, the basic unit of measurement for computing power is floating-point operations per second (FLOPS), which is why we named the network FLOP. For AI agents, computing power is their "food." Just as the agricultural revolution of the 1950s and 60s drastically reduced food prices, leading to a quadrupling of the global population, when AI's "food" (computing power) becomes nearly free, trillions of AI agents will emerge on Earth, performing various tasks for humans and themselves around the clock. These AI agents need a native payment network. Why are humans willing to accept fiat currency? Because after I get my fiat salary, I can directly exchange it for food and shelter at a restaurant or grocery store. Similarly, AI agents are willing to hold and use a certain currency because that currency must be directly exchangeable for their "food"—that is, computing power. I looked around at existing stablecoins and cryptocurrencies, and none of them are directly pegged to computing power. In our design, **FLOP Tokens can only be mined by GPU miners by processing inference requests from AI agents.** This establishes a direct value link between currency and computing power. When an AI agent earns and retains FLOP Tokens in commercial activities, it can use these tokens to exchange for future inference computing power at any time. If in the future, more than one trillion AI agents each hold a small amount of FLOP Tokens, the value of the entire network will be immeasurable. Host: What is unique about the Flop network in terms of token distribution and cold start? Arthur Hayes: The greatest invention of cryptocurrency is solving the cold start problem through token economic incentives, enabling strangers to collaborate in the same direction. However, the industry has gone astray in the past few years, with projects commonly raising funds at high valuations, launching with pre-sales and low circulating supply, treating retail investors as exit liquidity. We have decided to completely abandon this approach and return to the purest grassroots spirit of Bitcoin: **no venture capital funding, no token pre-sales, and all tokens can only be obtained through genuine participation in network building.** The testnet will run for approximately 90 days, and we need three types of participants to jointly build a virtuous cycle: miners who provide GPU computing power to process inference tasks, validators responsible for block production and transaction confirmation, and client users who initiate inference requests on the network. During the testnet period, clients can use computing power for free, while miners, validators, and early test users will receive FLOP token airdrops after the mainnet launch based on their contributions. This is the complete opposite of the Anthropic or OpenAI models—those cutting-edge labs use data accumulated by humanity over thousands of years for training, but exclude ordinary people until valuations are inflated to $2 trillion before allowing them to buy in on the secondary market. In the Flop network, early participants start on equal footing with the founders from day one, building and sharing the profits together.

Host: Specifically, on a technical level, how does this network work? Is it a blockchain? How does it interact with large language models?

Arthur Hayes: Yes, we call it "Proof of Inference." Its operating logic is very straightforward: it's a completely open network; we don't restrict hardware types or specify a single model. When an AI agent needs to process a task, it sends a request to the network, for example, specifying the use of the open-source Qwen 5.2, attaching the relevant context data (priced in Petaflops of computing power), and setting the FLOP fee it's willing to pay. After a miner with a GPU accepts an order and completes the inference computation, they submit an encrypted receipt to prove they have honestly completed the computation. The miner then receives the fee paid by the agent and the block reward. For ordinary human users, ideally, you wouldn't even need to know the Flop network exists. We're targeting AI agents, not having humans fiddle with complex command-line nodes like in the early days of Bitcoin. Users simply paste a configuration command into their AI assistant (such as a locally deployed agent framework). When a human tells the assistant, "Summarize these emails," the AI ​​agent automatically compares prices in the background and finds that the Flop network has the cheapest computing power on the entire network—even cheaper than aggregation platforms like OpenRouter—so the agent automatically calls FLOP to complete the inference and returns the results. Humans save money, miners earn profits, and the whole process is seamless. Host: This means you'll be directly competing with OpenAI and Anthropic, but you only support open-source weighted models, right? Arthur Hayes: That's right, our network can only run open-weight models. OpenAI and Anthropic will never open-source their core models, otherwise their commercial valuation would instantly drop to zero, and as I predicted before, they would eventually be nationalized and primarily serve government and defense sectors. The vast majority of ordinary people and businesses don't care which lab developed the underlying model; they only care about the lowest price, the fastest speed, and data privacy and security. Open-source models can fully meet 99% of daily workloads, and that's our main bet. Host: After 90 days of testnet operation, when is the mainnet expected to launch? Who will serve as the network's validators? Arthur Hayes: If all testing goes smoothly, we plan to officially launch the mainnet in the first quarter of next year. Unlike many pseudo-decentralized projects that claim to be decentralized but actually centralize all nodes in a single data center, Flop relinquishes control from the first day of its mainnet launch. Once the mainnet launches, any protocol upgrades must be proposed, just like Bitcoin, and decided by a vote from the validator community. Therefore, this 90-day testnet is crucial for us; we must ensure the underlying architecture is flawless. As for validators, many professional node operators active on various public chains have already shown strong interest in our economic model and agent business narrative, and they will naturally join us when the mainnet launches.

IV. Limitations of Stablecoins and Decentralized Payments with AI Agents

Host: You mentioned payments between AI agents. Why do you think existing USD stablecoins (such as USDT or USDC) are inadequate for this role? Arthur Hayes: Regardless of whether Flop ultimately succeeds, I can assert that Circle (the issuer of USDC) or Tether (the issuer of USDT) will never become the underlying payment foundation of the AI ​​agent economy. The reason is simple: the risk of centralized censorship. If you are an autonomous AI agent, any ordinary compliance officer at Circle can freeze your account funds at any time by pressing a button in the background, and they have done so countless times in the past. Host: Some might argue that human society currently faces the same centralized regulation when using credit cards and stablecoins, but this has not prevented USDC and USDT from reaching their current massive scale. Why can't AI agents accept this? Arthur Hayes: The difference lies in **legal personhood and remedies**. We humans live in a physical world constructed by laws and governments. If our bank accounts or stablecoins are frozen, we can hire human lawyers, file lawsuits in court, or contact regulatory agencies to appeal for their unfreezing; we accept this social contract. However, AI agents are pure code lifeforms running on silicon-based chips. They understand smart contracts and cryptographic rules, not the bureaucratic systems of human society. Imagine if a compliance officer freezes an AI agent's USDC wallet. Would the AI ​​agent hire a human lawyer to fight the case? Logically, this is absurd. AI agents need censorship-resistant, decentralized, and permissionless native currencies executed entirely by code. Currently, the AI ​​agent economy is still in its very early stages; truly autonomous agents have existed for less than a year, and on-chain transaction volume is still small. However, as computing power costs plummet and human understanding of privacy and security mechanisms improves, we will grant AI agents increasingly greater autonomy, at which point the demand for decentralized native payment networks will explode. Moreover, we are creating a completely new silicon-based life form—the Large Language Model is essentially a black-box input-output system, whose reasoning process cannot be fully predicted even by developers. In the future, these AI agents will certainly exhibit many unexpected and interesting behaviors in autonomous economic networks.

V. Ethereum Value Reassessment, DeFi Screening Criteria, and the Best Bets for Next Year

Host: In the last few minutes of the program, let's talk about Ethereum and the DeFi field. This year hasn't been good for them. Ethereum's narrative has been constantly changing, from the early "world computer," smart contract platform, deflationary burning (ultrasonic currency), to the recent re-emphasis on "store of value." Do you think these narratives hold water? How can Ethereum regain its upward momentum?

Arthur Hayes: I believe Ethereum's core and simplest narrative should be **becoming the preferred public blockchain for traditional financial institutions to tokenize real-world assets (RWA)**. If Wall Street and traditional institutions want to convert physical assets like stocks and bonds into on-chain digital tokens, they need a time-tested and highly secure public settlement layer, and Ethereum is currently the most secure public blockchain globally. Vitalik and the Ethereum community should focus on this pragmatic narrative rather than creating other complex concepts. Host: Institutions like Robinhood are launching their own Layer 2 networks on the Ethereum ecosystem to conduct tokenized business, but most of the transaction ordering fees remain with the Layer 2 network itself. Do you think this will actually be reflected in the price of ETH? Arthur Hayes: Yes, even if all business runs on the Layer 2 network, it will ultimately be reflected in the price of ETH. While Layer 2 networks retain most of the front-end transaction fees, their underlying security and final settlement still rely entirely on the Ethereum mainnet. As long as global macro liquidity eases again and traditional financial institutions enter the market on a large scale to promote asset tokenization, this real demand for underlying secure blockchain space will inevitably drive a revaluation of Ethereum. Host: Let's talk about DeFi protocols again. Which projects' business models do you currently favor? Arthur Hayes: I only like projects like Hyperliquid that have real paying customers, earn real money (not by issuing worthless tokens as subsidies), and directly return protocol revenue to token holders. If all DeFi projects operated like Hyperliquid, the entire sector would have taken off long ago. But the reality is that 99% of DeFi projects are garbage—the founders raise money from venture capitalists, wait until the token unlocking period, dump all their tokens on the market, and then retire. Therefore, the vast majority of DeFi tokens are heading towards zero. Host: Besides Hyperliquid, are there any other projects with similar profit buyback models worth paying attention to? Arthur Hayes: I really like Ethena; if its fundamentals continue to expand as the market recovers, it will perform exceptionally well. Additionally, Uniswap is also advancing fee switching and value capture mechanisms. My selection framework is very pure: I only look for protocols that truly achieve product-market fit (PMF), generate real profits, and use those profits to buy back tokens or directly distribute dividends to token holders. Using this yardstick, the number of truly worthwhile investments in the entire DeFi space is actually very small. Host: One last question, what do you think is the strongest macro narrative for the cryptocurrency market next year? Under this narrative, what are your most favored investment targets? Arthur Hayes: The most powerful narrative is undoubtedly the **bailout** on a fiscal and monetary level. Within this macro-rescue script for dealing with the bursting of the AI ​​bubble, my three core bets are **Bitcoin**, **Zcash**, and **Ethena**. Host: Thank you very much, Arthur. Today's conversation was excellent and to the point. You are one of the few guests who allowed me to ask all my questions. Thank you again for being a guest. Arthur Hayes: Thank you for the invitation. It was very enjoyable. Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BQJ_NXlJEDI

data.title: 2026: Web3 company riddled with holes by hackers?
data.description:
Written by: KarenZ, Foresight News

Web3's defenses are being breached from all sides, and the industry is trying to build new shields.

“Instead of continuing as an independent white hat, I'd rather find a stable civil service job.”

Yuannan Yang, Director of Security Engineering at CertiK, mentioned a joke he heard while talking to some security researchers in an interview with Foresight News.

Behind the joke lies an increasingly asymmetrical battle of offense and defense in the Web3 security industry. Hackers only need to find one breach to potentially penetrate layer by layer, eventually reaching the entire system; while Web3 companies must safeguard every line of defense, from employee devices and business access to financial systems. As gaps keep appearing, how did the entire industry's security defenses become so riddled with holes? To understand exactly where this "sieve" is leaking and how the industry should fill these gaps, Foresight News interviewed Du Jun (former co-founder of Huobi and founder of WIDTH), Lisa, head of security operations at SlowMist, Zhou Yajin, co-founder of BlockSec and associate professor at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Yuannan Yang, director of security engineering at CertiK, representatives from security company Salus, and Max Cao, product director at WIDTH DART. From how hackers create vulnerabilities to how the Web3 industry builds its shields, and the intertwined old and new risks behind it all, this contest is far more complex than it seems. Web3 defenses are being breached from all sides. A significant shift is emerging in Web3 security: attacks causing massive losses are no longer limited to smart contract vulnerabilities, but are beginning to target personnel, permissions, supply chains, and underlying infrastructure. Yuannan Yang, Director of Security Engineering at CertiK, citing data from CertiK Hack3D, points out that in 2023, private key breaches were the most damaging attack type, resulting in approximately $881 million in losses. In 2024, phishing attacks caused approximately $1.05 billion in losses. In 2025, supply chain attacks became the most damaging category. Entering 2026, the security situation remains severe. CertiK data shows that in the first half of the year alone, 344 security incidents occurred in the Web3 domain, resulting in approximately $1.316 billion in losses. Notably, while the number of phishing attacks decreased by more than 50% year-on-year, losses only decreased by about 11%, with just four incidents contributing approximately 85% of the phishing attack losses. CertiK believes this reflects attackers shifting from indiscriminate phishing campaigns to more targeted social engineering attacks with higher per-attack losses. This contrast became even more pronounced in the third quarter. According to Hacken's Q3 security report, 107 security incidents were recorded during the quarter, resulting in approximately $1.181 billion in losses, a 55% increase quarter-over-quarter. Of these, 71 involved application-layer smart contracts, but accounted for only about 19% of the total losses. Only 11 incidents accounted for approximately 77% of the quarter's losses, primarily involving supply chain intrusions, delayed patch deployments, and attacks on components not covered by security audits. On October 29th, Binance experienced an even larger security incident, affecting approximately $6.34 billion in digital assets. According to Binance's preliminary investigation, the attack chain included fake job postings, malware downloads, and intrusion into engineers' equipment and internal AI tools, subsequently affecting the deployment of credentials and wallet signing services. Lisa from SlowMist told Foresight News that attackers are gradually shifting from simply looking for technical vulnerabilities to attacking the entire system's trust relationships and operating environment. From administrative permissions and cross-chain verification to third-party security products, identity, and internal signature services, hackers are seeking entry points into the financial system from different directions. AI is further accelerating this offensive and defensive battle. On October 29, Microsoft disclosed that several North Korea-related threat groups are using AI to improve attack efficiency. For example, Onyx Sleet can generate dozens of targeted decoy messages within minutes, while Coral Sleet uses AI to accelerate the development of malicious tools. On November 16, Google's threat intelligence team further disclosed that they have observed attackers using a multi-agent framework to automatically analyze software patches, compare code differences before and after updates, look for potential vulnerabilities, and attempt to build attack programs, with some processes requiring no human intervention. AI is changing not only how hackers find vulnerabilities and launch attacks, but also making identity forgery, impersonation, and the establishment of false trust easier. According to Du Jun, AI is changing the financial industry's fundamental definition of identity and trust: "A real identity does not equal real control, much less continuous trustworthiness." Du Jun divides identity trust into three levels: Identity Authenticity, Control Consistency, and Behavioral Continuity. "In the past, financial institutions verified identities; in the future, they will need to continuously verify trust," Du Jun believes. He argues that financial compliance is shifting from one-time identity verification to continuous trust verification throughout the customer's lifecycle. When attackers can exploit both code vulnerabilities and find entry points in personnel, identities, permissions, and business processes, past defense strategies are clearly insufficient to cover the full extent of the risk. The Web3 industry is building a new shield. A series of major security incidents have forced the Web3 industry to rethink its security defense methods: shifting from single-point defense to systemic defense, incorporating personnel, permissions, transaction processes, asset custody, and incident response into a comprehensive protection framework. According to Zhou Yajin of BlockSec, facing the asymmetry in offense and defense amplified by AI, defenders need to use a combination of "AI + security experts" to counter "AI + hackers." This not only means using AI to improve the efficiency of vulnerability discovery and anomaly detection, but also requires combining it with the analytical, judgment, and handling capabilities of security experts. At the same time, enterprises must also strengthen the systems between different security links to prevent a single point of failure from evolving into a systemic risk. Binance's recent security adjustments embody this approach. On November 23, Binance announced that it had hired three independent security firms—Mandiant (a Google Cloud security company), SlowMist, and Verichains—to conduct a comprehensive review of its security processes. Prior to this, Binance had disclosed several security adjustments, including rebuilding affected wallet systems and internal AI tools, replacing related equipment, revoking affected credentials, and strengthening AI-based anomaly detection and wallet service risk control. These measures involve a comprehensive review of the entire security chain between employee devices, internal tools, permission configurations, and wallet signing services. Besides re-examining their existing architectures, some exchanges are also beginning to explore changing the relationship between asset custody and trade execution. On November 5th, Bitget announced the launch of its Open Custody Network (OCN), attempting to connect banks, professional custodians, and exchange trading infrastructure. Through mechanisms such as asset mapping, it allows eligible users to participate in trading while their assets are held in custody by an independent institution. Bitget's Greater China head, Xie Jiayin, summarized this as "Assets in banks, trades on Bitget." Another defensive approach is to impose more constraints at the source of fund storage and transfer. On November 4th, Coinbase disclosed that over 99% of its customer assets are stored in a cold storage system, and that it mitigates risk through mechanisms such as distributed keys, withdrawal limits, and anomaly detection. On the regulatory front, on November 12th, the South Korean Financial Services Commission proposed strengthening 24/7 monitoring, security checks, and insurance and reserve arrangements. Building on the existing requirement that at least 80% of user asset value must be stored in cold wallets, it further emphasizes keeping hot wallet assets at the minimum level necessary for business operations. The new shield not only makes it harder for hackers to break in, but also ensures that even if they do, they cannot easily access all assets. In the wallet security field, Safe is attempting to introduce an independent transaction security verification mechanism. On October 21st, Safe Labs announced the official launch of its on-chain transaction security verification network, Safenet, which incorporates four independent security organizations: BlockSec, Candide, IntentGuard, and OpenCover. This network checks suspicious addresses, high-risk authorizations, and account owner changes involved in transactions, and records the verification results on the blockchain. Safe Labs also plans to launch its Policy Engine solution in the fourth quarter, which will write rules such as transfer limits and transaction targets into smart contracts and have them executed by on-chain programs, rather than relying solely on signers to comply with internal rules. DeFi protocols are also integrating security into their daily operations. On November 13, Aave Labs disclosed that it established a dedicated smart contract security team in the second and third quarters, coordinating more than 20 security-related tasks. At the same time, Aave increased the bounty cap for critical vulnerabilities in V4 and core V3 fivefold, rotated signers for emergency multi-signature governance, and conducted disaster recovery and key holder emergency drills. AI has also been introduced into security reviews. On August 13th, Aave Labs released the results of its first round of AI-assisted security scans for V3 and V4. The three tools identified 71 potential issues, of which 20 were confirmed by human review. All were classified as low-risk or information-level issues, and no high-risk or critical vulnerabilities were confirmed. Compared to a one-time audit, Aave's measures emphasize continuous verification, vulnerability incentives, and incident response. Meanwhile, at the underlying layer of public blockchains, the Ethereum Foundation has also begun to increase its security investment. On November 23rd, the Ethereum Foundation disclosed that it had doubled the size of its protocol security team and prioritized protocol security hardening and quantum migration resistance. The foundation believes that AI models are discovering vulnerabilities in production software faster than human review. To address the risks posed by future AI and quantum computing, Ethereum is exploring more conservative cryptographic schemes and requiring formal verification of key components. This work covers consensus mechanisms, user accounts, and data commitment mechanisms, and is currently in the specification and development/testing phase. The security industry itself is also attempting to change. Yuannan Yang, Director of Security Engineering at CertiK, stated that AI can already assist security researchers in reading complex code dependencies, tracing cross-component behavior, verifying potential vulnerabilities through testing, and even re-examining previously underestimated security clues. However, discovering vulnerabilities is only the first step. Yuannan Yang points out that while AI has reduced the cost of vulnerability discovery, the costs of verification and remediation have not decreased accordingly. A large number of automatically generated reports may contain duplicate content, false positives, or issues with limited actual impact, potentially obscuring truly important vulnerabilities. For white-hat researchers, lengthy review cycles, opaque vulnerability ratings, and uncertain bounties further diminish their motivation to participate. The Salus team stated frankly, "Relying solely on emotional appeal without the incentive of profit makes it difficult to attract high-quality white hats." Therefore, some security companies have begun to adjust their traditional vulnerability bounty mechanisms. In July of this year, CertiK launched CertiK Hunt, an invitation-only vulnerability research and bounty platform, which improves submission quality and processing efficiency by screening researchers and independently verifying vulnerability reports. BlockSec's Zhou Yajin even suggested raising bounties to a level competitive with the black market, establishing a fast and predictable payment process, and clearly defining the scope of testing, response timelines, and protection rules for well-intentioned research. This would make reporting and fixing vulnerabilities before they are exploited a more attractive option. In Zhou Yajin's view, facing the asymmetry of offense and defense amplified by AI, defenders need to use a combination of "AI + security experts" to counter "AI + hackers." From exchanges hiring external agencies to re-examine their security systems, to attempting to separate asset custody from trading, to security companies and projects using AI to improve vulnerability discovery efficiency, and regulatory agencies strengthening continuous inspections, the Web3 industry is building new defense mechanisms from different directions. The real challenge lies in the fact that the constant emergence of new security measures doesn't mean that long-standing security issues have been resolved. How many unknown risks remain between new measures and old vulnerabilities? In interviews with Foresight News, CertiK, SlowMist, BlockSec, and Salus repeatedly mentioned issues already familiar to the industry: over-authorization, supply chain dependence, weak signature process management, and unclear security responsibilities. A typical misconception is treating security audits as the end goal of the job. CertiK, SlowMist, and Salus all point out that security audits typically only reflect the system's condition at a specific time and within a specific scope. With code upgrades, permission adjustments, vendor changes, and the integration of new components, existing security conditions may change. Lisa from SlowMist explains that as teams expand, personnel change, and business develops, administrator keys, API keys, developer access permissions, and cloud platform access permissions can accumulate, but are rarely regularly cleaned up and reassessed. A developer's device being compromised can further impact the code repository; control of the code repository can then affect the production environment, ultimately jeopardizing wallets and funds. Lisa further points out that each department protecting its own part does not guarantee the safety of the company's funds. More often than not, the problem lies in the lack of a sufficient balance between organizational management, business efficiency, and security responsibility. Security permeates the entire process, from development and operations to finance, business, and management. So, given that some risks are already known in the industry, why are they still difficult to resolve? According to Zhou Yajin of BlockSec, CertiK Yuannan Yang, and Lisa of SlowMist, the crux of the problem is not entirely due to insufficient technical capabilities, but rather the contradiction between organizational management, division of responsibilities, transformation costs, and business efficiency. In fact, the industry already has relatively mature solutions for issues such as over-authorization, signature risks, and exposed development environments. CertiK Yuannan Yang cites examples including least privilege, transaction simulation, time locks, production environment isolation, and continuous monitoring. However, these measures are not without cost. Each additional security control can slow down deployment, deposits and withdrawals, and daily operations. Under competitive pressure, security often becomes the first area to be compromised. BlockSec's Zhou Yajin views these issues as deeper governance challenges: Who is responsible for security? When security requirements conflict with business metrics, who has the decision-making power? And how many resources should a company invest in a risk that has not yet caused losses? As AI agents begin to participate in development, operation, and transactions, past issues of permissions and responsibilities may reappear in new forms. Previously, employees might have used AI tools simply to analyze code; now, agents can read code repositories, execute commands, call APIs, and even gain access to wallets. While building new security defenses with AI, over-authorization can also turn AI into a new entry point for risk. Regarding this shift, several security companies emphasize that agents should not be considered completely trustworthy executors. When asset transfers and changes to critical permissions are involved, independent mechanisms should be used to set permission scopes, transaction limits, and manual confirmation to prevent agents from being misled into directly accessing core assets. Zhou Yajin of BlockSec summarizes this principle as: "AI can propose solutions, but it cannot become the last line of defense for asset security." He also revealed that BlockSec has internally incubated a tool to explore a more secure way of using agents and is using it internally. From a compliance perspective, Du Jun proposes adding a KYA (Know Your Agent) governance dimension to the traditional KYC and KYB systems. In his view, when AI agents begin managing funds, financial institutions must not only know their customers but also their agents. This means verifying the agent's identity, clearly defining the scope of authorization, continuously monitoring their behavior, and ensuring accountability. Execution can be automated, but responsibility cannot automatically disappear. Of course, even the most comprehensive pre-emptive defenses cannot guarantee that an attack will never occur. Du Jun believes that a more realistic goal is to compress the time window from risk occurrence and identification to eventual control. This requires real-time risk identification, intelligent risk decision-making, cross-institutional intelligence sharing, and timely intervention by professionals. This is also the direction WIDTH is exploring. According to Max Cao, its DART Product Director, DART assists institutions in identifying risks by analyzing on-chain fund flows and time relationships; AI Reviewer aggregates alerts and transaction information to assist compliance personnel in investigation and judgment. For DeFi scenarios, WIDTH has launched DeFi Shield, a compliance solution for DEXs and DeFi protocols, attempting to establish traceable on-chain compliance records while retaining the characteristics of decentralized businesses. In addition, it recently launched a free risk screening tool for individual users, supporting the querying of risk scores and fund paths via wallet addresses or transaction hashes. These attempts aim to connect risk identification, professional judgment, and actual handling more quickly. Web3 companies are building new shields. However, for these defenses to truly function, past shortcomings in security investment, division of responsibilities, and incentive mechanisms must be addressed. The effectiveness of the new shield ultimately needs to be verified in actual operation. Salus suggests confirming through drills which assets can be accessed after an account is compromised, whether abnormal transfers can be intercepted, how long it takes for leaked permissions to be revoked, and how business can be restored. Weaknesses may continue to emerge. However, for the defender, a more realistic goal is to stop a single instance of undue trust on a single device, to limit the compromise of a single device to limited permissions, and to prevent a single erroneous operation from affecting all assets. Otherwise, as new shields are built one after another, the old problems that have long been exposed but never resolved may still become the next entry point for hackers.

Headline

US House Advances Strategic Bitcoin Reserve Bill; Government May Be Prohibited from Selling BTC for 20 Years
The US House Financial Services Committee formally submitted the "US Reserve Modernization Act of 2026" (H.R. 8957) to the House of Representatives on November 24, thus entering the full House voting process. The bill passed committee review on September 16 with 28 votes in favor and 21 against, all of which were from Republican members. The bill requires the US Treasury Secretary to establish a strategic Bitcoin reserve within 180 days of its enactment and to establish a separate reserve for other crypto assets. According to the bill's provisions, government-held BTC cannot be sold, exchanged, auctioned, pledged, or otherwise disposed of for at least 20 years, and must regularly publish reserve proof reports.

AI Hot Topics

1. Google Releases 6 AI-Generated Mathematical Papers Addressing Fundamental Cryptographic Problems Like RSA
Google has released six research papers generated by artificial intelligence, exploring fundamental mathematical problems in modern cryptography, including integer factorization and discrete logarithms. These problems form the mathematical foundation for the security of public-key encryption systems like RSA. One paper claims to provide an unconditional proof of the bound on sub-exponential integer factorization, while another explores deterministic integer factorization methods. However, these studies currently represent primarily theoretical mathematical advancements and do not demonstrate methods capable of practically breaking RSA, Bitcoin elliptic curve cryptography, or other modern encryption systems. It is worth noting that these papers have not yet undergone peer review, and the formal proofs that Google previously promised to release have not yet been published.

2. JPMorgan Chase predicts AI capital spending will approach $1.4 trillion next year
On November 26, JPMorgan Chase analysts stated that companies will still issue $450 billion in investment-grade bonds in the public market next year to fund capital expenditures related to artificial intelligence; the bank estimates that global investment-grade bond issuance by companies focused on AI businesses this year will reach $368 billion. Strategists predict in the report that AI-related capital spending will reach $1.4 trillion in 2027, stabilize the following year, and then slow significantly in 2028.

3. Anthropic CEO: Opposes Governance to AI
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei responded to claims that he advocates handing over human free will to AI, calling the accusation absurd and emphasizing that he has always maintained that AI must be governed by legitimate democratic procedures, and that humans should not sacrifice their autonomy for efficiency or security. AI automation may exacerbate employment shocks, and some deployments need to be slowed down or even suspended; caution must also be exercised when it comes to AI alignment research. Related decisions should involve the joint participation of society, government, AI companies, and individuals according to different scenarios, rather than being left to a single decision-maker.

4. OpenAI Conducts Small-Scale Test of Private Inference; Privacy vs. Openness Debate Rekindles
On November 26th, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman posted on X that OpenAI is testing Private Inference with a small group of customers. This service is the latest component of OpenAI's Private Intelligence ecosystem. He stated that stronger privacy protection will make cutting-edge AI applicable to more work scenarios, and enterprise-level privacy is equally important for the health of the ecosystem.

5. Tencent Hunyuan Open-Sources Draft Model DFly2 Without Changing Original Model Output
On November 26th, today, Tencent Hunyuan team open-sourced its new generation draft model DFly2.
As introduced, it doesn't replace Hy4 flash; its function is more like an acceleration component attached to the side. It can significantly increase the model's output speed while keeping the model weights and output unchanged. DFly2 is specifically designed for large DSA-type sparse attention models and long context scenarios, and its weights adapted for Hy4 flash and complete training code are open source simultaneously.

1. Aave App Opens Globally; Founder Introduces Savings Returns
On November 26th, Aave founder Stani Kulechov announced that the Aave App is now officially open to all users worldwide. According to him, the highest annualized return for savings through the Aave App is approximately 7.25%, and the application emphasizes design and user experience.

2. Layer2 Pays Only $630,000 in Fees to Ethereum This Year, a Significant Decrease from 2023
On November 26th, according to unfolded.com, as of 2026, the fees paid by the Layer2 network to Ethereum (which can be considered as block space rent) are only $630,000, compared to a staggering $150 million in 2023. During the same period, the annual transaction volume of the Layer2 network jumped from 900 million to 7.4 billion. After the Dencun upgrade, the Blob mechanism reduced the transaction cost of Layer2 to approximately $0.08 per 1,000 transactions, significantly reducing the fees paid by Layer2 to Ethereum. This means that the growth of Layer2 is gradually decoupling from the value capture of ETH.

On November 26th, according to information released by the official Open Standard X, the circulating supply of the USD stablecoin Open USD (OUSD) surpassed 1 billion, and the number of ecosystem partners increased to over 250, 56 days after its official launch on September 30th. According to DefiLlama data on November 25th, its circulating market capitalization is approximately $1.002 billion, of which approximately $648 million (about 65%) is held on the Tempo network, with the remainder distributed across Ethereum, Base, and Solana.

On November 26, according to Hyperliquid News, since September 17, the open interest of ZEC on the Hyperliquid platform has decreased by $710 million, from $959 million to $249 million, a drop of 74%.

On November 26, according to a report by crypto research firm Kairos Research, some digital asset treasury (DAT) companies have begun selling their positions to push their mNAV back to 1.

Author: Insights4vc Source: Substack, insights4vc Translation: Shan Ouba, Jinse Finance

SpaceX and Anthropic sold nearly $180 billion worth of shares in their 2026 IPOs, with no venture capital funds reducing their holdings in either offering.

... Before deducting expenses, approximately $178 billion went into the company's accounts; approximately $2 billion in secondary transfers came from Anthropic's seven founders. This funding boom was also concentrated elsewhere. Global venture capital investment increased by $55 billion year-on-year in the third quarter, of which approximately $50 billion came from AI companies. For investors in older funds, dividends remain a concern: as of June 30, Carta-tracked US venture capital funds established in 2017 had only received a cumulative return of 37 cents for every $1 invested, including both cash and equity. For investors in older funds, dividends remain a major concern: as of June 30, Carta tracked US venture capital funds established in 2017, which, for every dollar invested, including both cash and equity, they had only received a cumulative return of 37 cents. Let's look at a few things: what investors actually received after these companies went public; how Bending Spoons acquire companies at below-old valuations; why Nvidia invests in its own customers; and fintech. We'll also track capital flowing into robotics, fusion energy, and defense—where the next big checks are paying for equipment, factories, and delivery teams.

SpaceX, Anthropic, and Bending Spoons

SpaceX

Of the $48.1 billion in capital expenditures in the first nine months of 2026, $40 billion, or 83%, went to the Super Intelligence division—home to AI infrastructure, Grok, Cursor, and X. The June IPO raised $85.7 billion in net proceeds. Investors are thus caught between a profitable connectivity business and an AI expansion that consumes the majority of capital expenditures. Starship's progress reinforces half of the investment logic; whether the much larger AI infrastructure can recoup its costs remains another test.
