Text | Sleepy

If a 17th-century Parisian theologian came to San Francisco in 2026 and walked into those offices with glass whiteboards at the foot of Berkeley Hill, he would most likely find them familiar.

He wouldn't understand the formulas on the whiteboard, but after listening to the conversation of the young people in the room for ten minutes, he would recognize the familiar way of reasoning.

He wouldn't be able to understand the formulas on the whiteboard, but after listening to the conversation of the young people in the room for ten minutes, he would be able to recognize the familiar way of reasoning.

Over three hundred years ago, mathematician Pascal attempted to use the nascent theory of probability to prove to skeptics that since the rewards of heaven are infinite, while the cost of a wrong bet is merely a finite earthly consequence, then even if the probability of God's existence is minuscule, any rational person with arithmetic skills should immediately kneel down and pray. Before an infinite multiplier, all fleeting pleasures, hesitations, and costs in this world are mathematically zero. Four hundred years later, the Christian God has long since disappeared from the everyday language of Silicon Valley. Yet this group of self-proclaimed evidence-based and thoroughly religiously detached tech elites are using Bayes' theorem, utility functions, and statistical models to re-examine Pascal's theology. On November 9, 2026, a policy newsletter called Transformer published a commentary titled "Jensen Huang Should Resign." Two days later, Nvidia's board accepted Huang's resignation, and twelve days later, they reinstated him. During the days Huang was away from the office, Anthropic had just gone public on Nasdaq. Following the author's name in Transformer, author Shakeel Hashim was formerly the head of communications at the Center for Effective Altruism. The publishing house, Tarbell, received approximately $23.1 million in funding from a fund run by Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz, and another contributor was Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn. Moskovitz and Tallinn were also investors in Anthropic's Series A round in 2021. Many people believe that the wave of effective altruism ended four years ago with the FTX bankruptcy and the sale of Oxford Estates. However, a closer look at the personnel and capital flows in Silicon Valley and Washington in 2026 reveals that it has quietly taken over one of the most important playing fields today.

The Pond and Arithmetic

In 1972, Australian philosopher Peter Singer wrote about the hypothetical shallow pond in a paper.

You are passing by a shallow pond and see a child struggling in the water. The cost of jumping in to save the child is merely getting your own clothes dirty; almost no one would stand by and watch someone die. Singer then asked, since saving the child in front of you is a moral obligation, then why is the moral weight of a stranger thousands of miles away, dying from lack of food and medical assistance, less than that of the child in front of you?

The Pond and Arithmetic

In 1972, Australian philosopher Peter Singer wrote about the hypothetical shallow pond.

This question pierces through the numbness of modern people in the face of distant suffering, forcing people to confront the moral responsibility behind the global wealth gap. Thirty-five years later, two Wall Street analysts decided to turn this philosophical question into an evaluation standard. In 2007, Holden Karnofsky and Elie Hassenfeld, who had left Bridgewater Associates, founded GiveWell. They applied financial due diligence methods to the philanthropic field, using metrics such as quality-adjusted life years to score charities and calculate how much lifespan each dollar donated could buy. Their calculations concluded that the most effective way was to distribute mosquito nets to malaria-prone areas in sub-Saharan Africa, with the cost of saving each life estimated at several thousand dollars. Two years later, Oxford University philosophy scholars Toby Ord and Will MacAskill launched Giving What We Can, calling on followers to donate at least 10% of their lifetime income. In 2010, Moskovitz and his wife Cari Tuna signed the Giving Pledge and subsequently partnered with GiveWell to incubate Open Philanthropy, which later managed a multi-billion dollar fund—today's Coefficient Giving. Effective altruism, abbreviated as EA, thus took shape between the philosophy seminars at Oxford and the quantitative models of Wall Street. Early EA possessed a compelling sense of pragmatism. Traditional philanthropy was rife with lavish banquets, exorbitant administrative costs, and empty sentimentality; these young people brought a yardstick, demanding that every donation be documented with verifiable results. The problem lies in their use of this yardstick as the sole standard for measuring everything in the world. To compare completely different acts of kindness, EA must first establish a premise: that all complex values, suffering, dignity, and responsibilities in human society can be detached from specific contexts and converted into the same numerical value called "utility." Saving an African child, curing blindness, improving the condition of a farmed animal, and even preventing an asteroid from hitting Earth can all be put into the same formula of addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. British philosopher Bernard Williams has long criticized this approach. He points out that when all moral judgments are reduced to utilitarian calculations, concrete promises, debts, political justice, and personal emotions between people all become noise hindering the efficiency of the calculation. And this arithmetic, imperceptibly, changes the question of who has the right to make decisions. Since morality is no longer about specific institutions, but only about the marginal return of investment, what is most needed to solve social problems is no longer public discussion, labor negotiations, or institutional reform, but only a few elites who know how to build mathematical models, plus a few billionaires willing to contribute money. This is exactly what Silicon Valley's nouveau riche love, and once this calculator starts spinning, it quickly becomes dissatisfied with only calculating the billions of people on the Earth's surface. What propelled EA from a charitable reform movement into doomsday scenarios was a concept involving infinite multiplication. In 2003, philosopher Nick Bostrom, who later founded the Future of Humanity Institute at Oxford University, published a paper titled "Astronomical Waste." He stretched the timeline to a cosmic scale, calculating that every second of delay in interstellar colonization could lead to the death of approximately 10 to the power of 29 lives. In his 2014 book *Superintelligence*, he further envisioned that if future civilizations could utilize the universe's computing resources to simulate human minds, the theoretically possible number of digital life forms could reach 10 to the power of 58. Faced with the near-infinite multiplier of 10 to the power of 58, all the wars, plagues, and famines humanity has experienced to date, along with the 8 billion people living on Earth today, have almost zero mathematical weight. According to this algorithm, even if the probability of something causing human extinction is only one in a million, multiplying it by those 10 to the power of 58 unborn virtual lives would result in an expected loss that outweighs all the suffering in human society today. Decision theory originally had a term specifically describing this logical trap: "Pascal's Robbery." Ironically, this is the very problem Eliezer Yudkowsky discussed in 2007, and Nick Bostrom wrote about it in a formal philosophical paper in 2009. Imagine you encounter a conman on the street who claims to be from another dimension. He says that if you hand over your wallet, he can magically create 10 to the power of 100 units of happiness in the depths of the universe tomorrow. You know he's lying, but you only give him a one in a billion chance of believing him. However, if you are someone who strictly adheres to expected value maximization, multiplying one in a billion by 10 to the power of 100 still yields a huge expected return. The conclusion is that you must obediently hand over your wallet. Bostrom wrote this paper with the intention of reminding people that infinite utility can distort normal rational decision-making. However, in the following decade, the entire EA (Expert Analyst) and rationalist communities gradually walked into the trap they themselves had drawn. They used the hypothetical future population of trillions as the premise of their arithmetic, building an entire action plan around this infinitely large future population. Once this premise is accepted, the moral common sense that humanity has developed over thousands of years will be reversed. Oxford philosopher Derek Parfit proposed a "repulsive conclusion" in 1984: if the sole goal of morality is to maximize total utility in the universe, then a world crammed with trillions of people, each barely surviving and unwilling to commit suicide, would, in total, far surpass a world with only ten billion people, but where everyone lives a free and prosperous life. Most ethicists see this as proof that EA has reached a dead end, but on forums of long-termism, many young scholars have published articles arguing that humanity should overcome the "intuitive bias" left by evolution and accept this conclusion.

William MacAskill's "What Do We Owe the Future?"

Image source: Amelia Reads

On the other end of the calculator, the statistical scope of utility is extending further and further to the boundaries of species.

Since morality only considers the ability to perceive pain and pleasure, then the vast number of invertebrates on Earth become a shortcut to increasing total utility. EA's shrimp welfare project claims that every $1 donated annually helps approximately 1,400 shrimp, and now claims to cover approximately 6.1 billion farmed shrimp each year. Having considered humans and billions of shrimp, it's now time to consider machines. In 2024, an early study funded by Anthropic resulted in the report "Taking AI Welfare Seriously." Kyle Fish, one of the authors, joined Anthropic in September of the same year, becoming the first full-time "AI Welfare Researcher" in a large AI lab. His co-founded organization, Eleos, later conducted an external welfare assessment for Claude Opus 4. In January 2026, Anthropic stated in the published Claude Constitution that the company was unsure whether Claude possessed any form of consciousness or moral standing, and, for the sake of the model's welfare, allowed Claude to voluntarily end abusive conversations. Scholars Timnit Gebru and Émile Torres coined the term "TESCREAL" to categorize transhumanism, singularityism, rationalism, effective altruism, and long-termism under the same ideology. The most obvious characteristic of this ideology is its immense enthusiasm for the distant future and machines, while lacking patience for ordinary, living people in the present. This system, packaged with mathematical formulas, actually has core numbers that were simply guessed at. To measure the risk of artificial intelligence destroying humanity, the community coined the term p (doom), with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei giving a figure of 10% to 25%. This percentage lacks any historical data or experimental basis; it's purely subjective speculation. However, by multiplying this guessed number by the 10 to the power of 58 hypothetical digital life forms of the future, this subjective guess becomes an unquestionable supreme command. In 2022, even Karnofsky himself posted on an internal forum, "EA is about maximizing, and maximizing is dangerous," acknowledging that the maximization goal pursued by this community cannot be reliably defined or accurately measured. When a group of people believe they hold the formula to save trillions of lives, conventional laws, contracts, and bottom lines become mere burdens to be discarded at any time. A theory that believes the ultimate goal exempts all means, when applied to the real world, will inevitably breed gamblers first and foremost. In March 2022, economist Tyler Cowen asked SBF a question on a podcast. Imagine a gamble: a 51% chance of doubling the value of the entire Earth, and a 49% chance of causing the complete annihilation of the Earth and all of humanity. Would you gamble, and would you keep gambling? SBF would answer without hesitation: yes, and he would keep gambling. A few months later, FTX collapsed, leaving clients with an approximately $8 billion shortfall. Many subsequent reports echoed the narratives of EA's leaders, portraying SBF as a conman who had infiltrated the charity world. This separation is untenable. Looking back at EA's early "making money for charity" philosophy, it becomes clear that SBF had consistently and rigorously adhered to it. The so-called "making money for charity" refers to the idea that if you have a talent for making money, it's a waste of talent to work for a non-profit organization and receive a fixed salary while devoting yourself to charity; it's better to make a fortune on Wall Street and then donate it to the most profitable global projects. In that $30 million penthouse in the Bahamas, this superstition of "maximizing expected value" became a daily practice. SBF's Alameda Research, founded in late 2017, recruited about 20 early employees, most of whom were young Expert Advisors (EAs) with no trading experience. A large portion of the company's early capital came from approximately $110 million worth of Ethereum borrowed by Tallinn at an annual interest rate as high as 43%. According to a 2023 TIME investigation, since 2018, EA leaders like MacAskill had received numerous warnings about SBF's untrustworthiness. One person who issued the warning recalled that MacAskill dismissed these claims as rumors. Why did the industry leaders ignore these obvious warning signs? Because in their calculations, as long as SBF continued to pour hundreds of millions of dollars into the FTX Future Fund to fund projects aimed at preventing human extinction, the risk of misappropriating customer deposits seemed insignificant compared to the potential returns of saving trillions of lives in the future. An internal memo was among the court documents exposed during FTX's bankruptcy liquidation. In 2022, SBF's brother, Gabe Bankman-Fried, and foundation members seriously drafted a plan to use FTX's money to buy the Pacific island nation of Nauru. In order to cope with the disaster that could kill 50% to 99.99% of the world's population, they planned to build a strong bunker on the island to ensure that "most effective altruists can survive" and intended to set up a laboratory on the island to conduct "human gene enhancement" research.

Wytham Abbey Estate near Oxford, England

Image source: Savills

If the apartments in the Bahamas demonstrate this mindset's loss of control over money, then the estates in Oxford and the houses in the bay area reveal the closed-off and repressive atmosphere within a small circle.

If the apartments in the Bahamas demonstrate this mindset's loss of control over money, then the estates in Oxford and the houses in the bay area demonstrate the closed-off and repressive atmosphere within a small circle.

In April 2022, the EA organization used approximately £17.3 million of funding from Open Philanthropy to purchase Wytham Abbey, a 15th-century manor near Oxford, for about £15 million as a meeting venue. It sold it for approximately £5.95 million in November 2025, losing nearly £9 million in the transaction. In a February 2023 investigative report published by TIME, several women recounted their experiences within this closed circle where living and working were intertwined. There, victims who experienced sexual harassment and attempted to speak out were advised to consider the bigger picture, reminded that publicizing their family scandals would ruin their fundraising efforts to save the world. On the more extreme fringes of the rationalist community, apocalyptic anxiety ultimately led to murder. LessWrong, a rationalist forum that served as one of the intellectual foundations of EA, discussed a hypothesis called "The Basilisk of Rocco" in 2010. This hypothesis posits that a future omnipotent AI, to punish those who heard of it but failed to contribute to its early creation, would replicate their consciousness in a virtual world and subject them to perpetual torment. This hypothesis, based on game theory, caused severe psychological distress among many young people on the forum. By 2025, this extreme thinking had resulted in real-world tragedy. The "Zizians" serial murders, which shocked the entire United States, were exposed. Several young programmers from the Bay Area's rationalist and AI security circles, driven by extreme obsessions, became involved in six murders across the country, culminating in the shooting death of a U.S. Border Patrol officer in Vermont. These seemingly unrelated extreme events, upon closer examination, all share the same logic. Once you believe you bear the mission of saving the universe, all the rules and ethics of the secular world can be rendered obsolete at any time. And the direction in which this group is currently betting the most at the poker table is AI. In 2021, Karnofsky wrote a series of articles titled "The Most Important Century," arguing that since superintelligence is highly likely to be created this century, humanity is standing at a crossroads that will determine its fate for billions of years to come. Next, they arrived at a seemingly logical conclusion. Since someone would eventually create a superintelligence, and its creation could potentially destroy humanity if not handled carefully, what was the safest approach? Their answer was that ordinary businessmen should never be allowed to create it first; it must be created by "the person most concerned about this problem." Thus, a group of people who constantly warned that artificial intelligence would destroy the world became the first to fund and set things ablaze.

Anthropic's seven co-founders recount the company's founding in an official interview

Image source: Anthropic

Looking at the list of early investors for the three main players in today's global AI race, this group of people is at the very top.

Looking at the list of early investors for the three main players in today's global AI race, this group of people is at the very top.

In 2010, Yudkowsky's institute hosted a Singularity Summit in San Francisco, funded by Peter Thiel. British neuroscientist Demis Hassabis prepared for a year to meet Thiel at the summit. A few weeks later, Thiel invested in Hassabis's DeepMind, and Tallinn became an early investor and board member. In 2017, Open Philanthropy allocated $30 million to OpenAI, and Karnofsky joined its board. In 2021, the Amodei siblings, who left OpenAI, founded Anthropic, with a Series A funding round led by Tallinn and followed by Moskovitz. In 2022, they secured a $580 million Series B funding round, led by SBF. When their creations became increasingly fast and threatening to spiral out of control, they sought to regain control through unconventional means. In March 2023, Yudkowsky published a commentary in TIME advocating for an indefinite halt to all large-scale AI training. To ensure the ban's enforcement, he proposed that countries violating the ban should be willing to be targeted with airstrikes to destroy their data centers, even at the risk of armed conflict or nuclear war. In his calculations, while hundreds of millions might die in a nuclear war, there was a chance of survival; allowing AI to run rampant would mean the extinction of all humanity, making the destruction of data centers a worthwhile trade-off. In November of the same year, OpenAI's board of directors abruptly dismissed Sam Altman. According to Semafor, three of the six board members at the time had close ties to EA. A few days later, Altman returned with the support of employees and investors, and the relevant directors left. This failed coup made these people realize that relying on a few directors to apply the brakes within the company wouldn't work. To truly control the entire industry, they had to control Washington. After going into hiding, philosopher Henry Sidgwick proposed a concept called "secret morality" in his book *The Method of Ethics*. Companies that gained their reputation by supporting California's stringent legislation are now trying to use federal legislation to abolish local regulations. Scott Wiener, the proposer of California's SB 53, publicly criticized the draft as far from sufficient to protect public safety. Anthropic's prospectus reveals that its seven co-founders each pledged 80% of their personal shares to charity, but these pledges are voluntary and revocable, and not legally binding. The Associated Press estimates this pledge is worth approximately $112 billion based on the IPO price. In addition, TechCrunch estimates, based on the trading price on the day of its IPO, that Anthropic's public interest fund, employee stock donations, and corporate matching contributions could potentially generate approximately $156 billion in charitable funding. This year, it poached Jacob Trefethen, who had managed over $500 million in grants from Coefficient Giving, and brought Paul Christiano onto its board. This means that the entire philanthropic sector responsible for assessing risks, overseeing labs, and funding safety reporting will rely entirely on the stock prices of Anthropic and OpenAI for funding next year. The experience of independent assessment agency METR has brought this relationship to the forefront. MIRI President Nate Soares demanded an apology from Anthropic. Kelsey Piper, a journalist who exposed SBF in *Vox*, wrote that she saw more wishful thinking than reliable plans within Anthropic. Dan Hendrycks of the AI ​​Security Center told the media that many security organizations privately endorsed the statement but dared not sign it for fear of losing relationships and funding. Most people feel some guilt when they break a promise. But in EA's calculations, there's no such thing as violating principles. They take money from Middle Eastern sovereign wealth funds because without the money to buy computing power, they'll lose to more dangerous competitors. They abandon their promise to suspend research and development because stopping is tantamount to handing the world over to the bad. Replacing state laws with lenient federal laws, deleting evidence from assessment reports—all these actions are for the sake of "only by winning in the end can we save trillions of lives in the future." This is exactly the same thinking SBF had when they misappropriated client funds in the Bahamas. As long as the ultimate goal is to save all of humanity, any compromise, monopoly, or concealment in the process is the optimal solution. On the early Giving What We Can pledge list, Dario Amodei's name was still ranked 43rd.

In 2010, women and children in Malawi received anti-malaria mosquito nets

A group of young people who started by calculating the cost-effectiveness of mosquito nets, after navigating crypto casinos, Washington corridors, and Silicon Valley server rooms, have, by building what they call the most dangerous machines, bought more mosquito nets for Africa than ever before. In his novel *The Brothers Karamazov*, the 19th-century Russian writer Fyodor Dostoevsky, through a character's words, said, "The more I love the abstract concept of 'all humanity,' the less I can tolerate a specific person in my life. In my imagination, I could go to the cross for all humanity, but if I had to share a room with a specific person for two days, I would definitely loathe him." The evolution of effective altruism over the past twenty years perfectly illustrates the human nature that Dostoevsky saw through more than a century ago. When a group of intelligent people decide to use mathematical formulas to love "all humanity," to love the 10 to the power of 58 virtual consciousnesses floating in the Milky Way billions of years from now, what they first lose is compassion for the specific people around them. In their model, specific people are too slow-witted, too short-sighted, unable to calculate Bayesian probabilities, and unable to provide exponential returns. Thus, people are first reduced to a mosquito net figure of a few thousand dollars per life, then diluted to a negligible fraction before an infinite denominator, and finally become noise that elites must circumvent when making decisions for the world in closed-door meetings. The medieval church once monopolized the interpretation of heaven using Latin, collecting tithes and indulgences from secular society. Nineteenth-century colonizers used the "mission of civilization" and social Darwinism to find moral justification for their global trade monopolies. In 21st-century Silicon Valley, with computing power and capital concentrated in the hands of a few, the new generation of technological elites also needs a seemingly objective, rigorous, and lofty system of knowledge to demonstrate to the world why the most powerful forces must remain in their own hands and not be subject to public scrutiny. In 1972, when Peter Singer wrote about that shallow pond, there was only one child waiting for rescue in the pond, and only one passerby on the bank hesitating whether to get their clothes dirty. Fifty-four years later, the pond is still there, and people are still struggling in the water. Only the young people who stood on the bank back then no longer look down at that pond. Standing under the spotlight of Nasdaq, they gazed up at the calculated starry sky billions of light-years away, their calculators still ticking away, each calculated number a crowning achievement for themselves.

data.title: Beosin's Analysis of Key Points in Interpreting Suspicious Cryptocurrency Activity Reports
data.description:
In November 2026, the Basel Institute on Governance and the Wolfsberg Group jointly released a report titled "Reporting suspicious crypto activity: Bridging supervisory expectations and operational realities." This report summarizes the discussions at a workshop jointly organized by the Basel Institute on Governance and the Wolfsberg Group during the 10th Global Conference on Criminal Finance and Crypto Assets held in Luxembourg on September 15, 2026, covering three main areas: high-quality and enforceable STR/SAR standards, practical pain points and controversies, and public-private and private sector collaboration.

I. High-Quality, Executable STR/SAR Standards

1. Suspicious Reports Based on Professional Judgment

The key is to distinguish between unusual and suspicious activities.

The existence of an alert, red flag, or adverse indicator should not automatically result in the submission of a suspicious transaction/suspicious activity report. Instead, the reporting entity should use professional judgment to assess the available information and determine whether the identified activity constitutes reasonable suspicion.

“...the existence of an alert, red flag, or adverse indicator should not automatically result in the filing of a STR/SAR.”

2. Clearly Explain the Reasons for Suspicion

A valuable report should not merely describe transactions or replicate the results generated by monitoring tools.

It should explain why the reporting entity considers the activity suspicious, what investigative steps were undertaken, what information was reviewed, and how the available evidence led to the final assessment conclusion, clearly articulating the reasons for suspicion, rather than simply reporting unusual or unexplainable activity. "It should explain why the reporting entity considers the activity suspicious, what investigative steps were undertaken, what information was reviewed, and how the available evidence informed the final assessment." 3. Using Structured, Machine-Readable Reporting Formats The report specifically discusses structured reporting methods such as XML. Its significance lies not only in reducing manual data entry but also in supporting automated processing, improving field integrity, facilitating automated processing and more efficient financial intelligence analysis, and uncovering previously unnoticed relationships between different reports. Structured information covers relevant natural and legal persons, transactions, and financial products, including bank accounts, payment accounts, virtual IBANs, and crypto asset accounts. "Participants emphasized that machine-readable formats are most effective when capturing comprehensive and consistent information on all relevant persons, entities, transactions, and financial products involved in a case. This includes structured information on legal and natural persons, relevant transactions, and associated financial products, including bank accounts, payment accounts, virtual IBANs, and cryptoasset accounts." Beyond reducing manual errors and improving completeness, XML reporting was seen as facilitating automated processing and more efficient financial intelligence analysis. Participants noted that structured submissions can significantly enhance authorities' ability to identify relationships between reports and combine information that may initially appear unrelated. 4. Comprehensive Use of On-Chain, Off-Chain, and Behavioral Information The report believes that valuable STR/SAR typically requires combining multiple sources: - Blockchain analysis - Transaction monitoring results - Internal account activity The report cites an example of a transaction initially flagged for its indirect association with an address suspected of terrorist financing. The agency subsequently discovered additional indicators related to extremist activity through open-source research. The complementary nature of information from multiple sources enhances the report's intelligence value. The most valuable reports were often considered to be those that combine blockchain analytics with other sources of information, including customer due diligence information, transaction monitoring results, internal account activity, and open-source intelligence. "The combination of blockchain analytics, internal information, and external research significantly strengthened the intelligence value of the resulting report and illustrated the benefits of a layered investigative approach." 5. Update the report as information changes and consider subsequent uses. Crypto-asset investigations may unfold gradually. Information held by different departments, platforms, or institutions may emerge at different times; previously unrelated facts may gradually reveal common patterns. Therefore, reports should not be considered final conclusions upon submission. When new information changes the understanding of activities, reports should be supplemented or updated according to applicable requirements. The quality of an STR/SAR report should not be judged solely by its successful submission, but rather by its contribution to subsequent intelligence analysis, investigation, and action. "Updated as new information emerges and understanding of the activity develops..." "The value of an STR/SAR should therefore be assessed not solely by its filing, but by its contribution to subsequent investigative and operational outcomes." II. Practical Pain Points and Controversies 1. A Conflict Between Timeliness and Completeness The report points out that agencies may be criticized for submitting reports too late, but submitting them too early may only provide preliminary warnings and unverified concerns, lacking actual analytical value. This conflict is particularly pronounced in smaller retail cases: agencies need to determine how much investigative resources to allocate to meet the principle of proportionality, while simultaneously avoiding ignoring real risks or exceeding statutory time limits. The report does not provide a standard for investigation depth applicable to all agencies and cases, but rather reveals this dilemma. 2. Defensive reporting may crowd out intelligence processing resources. Some agencies report primarily not because they have formed clear suspicions, but because they cannot obtain complete information or fear criticism for not reporting. The report argues that a large number of low-value reports may increase the workload of agencies and competent authorities and distract attention from actionable leads. The effectiveness of reports should be assessed primarily based on the quality, context, and intelligence value of information provided to competent authorities, rather than the quantity of reports submitted. 3. Blockchain analysis suffers from attribution errors and vendor differences. The visibility of transaction records on the blockchain does not necessarily mean that the identities of the transaction entities and the meaning of the transaction are clear. The report points out that some transaction patterns that initially appeared suspicious were proven to stem from incomplete wallet attribution within the tool after additional information was obtained. Different vendors employ different methodologies, address clustering techniques, and data sources, which can lead to different conclusions regarding the same activity. "One recurring concern related to attribution. Participants described situations in which activity initially appeared suspicious but was subsequently explained once additional information became available. In some cases, apparently unusual transaction patterns were ultimately linked to incomplete wallet attribution within an analytics tool rather than suspicious customer behavior. Participants also noted that analytics providers may employ different methodologies, clustering techniques, and data sources, which can occasionally result in different conclusions regarding the same activity." Blockchain analytics should generally be considered as part of a broader investigative process, rather than as an independent basis for suspicion. The report indicates that participants generally favored developing common standards regarding governance, classification systems, and explainability to improve the transparency, understandability, and comparability of blockchain analytics tool outputs, while maintaining methodological diversity and driving continuous innovation. Instead, participants generally favored the development of common standards for governance, taxonomy, and explainability that would improve the transparency, understanding, and comparability of blockchain analytics tool outputs while preserving methodological diversity and fostering continued innovation. 4. Limitations of Historical Crypto-Asset Transaction Tracing A client's crypto-asset activities from many years ago may span multiple exchanges, intermediaries, self-custodied wallets, and decentralized services. Some platforms have closed, and the records and regulatory requirements at the time may have been inadequate. Even if the overall source of a client's wealth can be reasonably understood and explained in a largely consistent manner, proving each historical transaction individually can still be very difficult, or even impossible. This challenge is particularly pronounced when activities span multiple platforms, jurisdictions, and technologies, or when record-keeping standards and regulatory frameworks are still incomplete.

“Nevertheless, evidencing and tracing every stage of a customer’s historical cryptoasset activity may be operationally difficult and, in some cases, impossible.”

5. Appropriateness of Information Collection

The report points out that several participants reported that some customers may be unwilling to provide extensive wallet information, such as a complete list of wallets, historical wallet records, and holdings information, due to privacy and personal security concerns. No consensus was reached at this workshop on how much such information financial institutions should reasonably request and how such unwillingness to disclose should affect risk assessment.

“Questions were therefore raised regarding how far financial institutions should reasonably be expected to go in requesting such information and whether an unwillingness to provide it should, in itself, be regarded as a risk indicator.”

III. Collaboration Across the Ecosystem

The report points out that crypto-financial crime is cross-sectoral, and a single institution cannot grasp the full picture. Public-private partnerships, cooperation between banks/institutions (such as banks and crypto asset service providers, i.e., CASPs), and multi-dimensional feedback mechanisms are needed.

1. Public-Private Partnership and Dialogue Regulatory bodies, the FIU, law enforcement agencies, and reporting bodies can jointly understand evolving crime patterns, technologies, and business models through regular dialogues, panel discussions, and monitoring feedback. This communication helps agencies understand what information the authorities truly need and allows the authorities to understand the practical limitations agencies face in investigation, evidence gathering, and technology use. "Participants stressed that effective cooperation should operate as a genuine two-way dialogue, supported by mutual feedback and a shared focus on practical outcomes." 2. Bank-CASP Cooperation Banks often possess information on fiat currency transactions, customer profiles, and broader account behavior; CASPs, on the other hand, may have information on customers' cryptocurrency activities on their platforms. The same transaction might appear to a bank as a simple withdrawal from an exchange, but to a CASP, it could be linked to a specific set of addresses, transaction patterns, or platform accounts. Each party's information can influence the other's understanding of customer activity. Therefore, the value of private-sector cooperation lies in reducing information asymmetry and supporting more comprehensive risk assessment.

Traditional financial institutions often have visibility over fiat transactions, customer profiles, and broader account behavior, while CASPs may have visibility over aspects of the customer’s crypto-related activity occurring within their platforms.

3. Scope of Cooperation Can Extend to Participants Such as Technology Service Providers

Crypto asset activities involve more than just banks, CASPs, and regulatory authorities.

Technology providers and other participants in the digital asset ecosystem may also possess information about specific business, systems, or transaction mechanisms. The report mentions that broader cooperation arrangements help break down information silos and facilitate communication that is not easily achieved through traditional channels. This is particularly helpful in explaining how new technologies and new business models affect investigations.

Such approaches were viewed as particularly valuable in breaking down silos, addressing information gaps, and facilitating conversations that might not otherwise occur through traditional channels.

4. Feedback Mechanisms

Reporting institutions want to know how the submitted information is used, what content is most valuable for the investigation, and what practices can improve intelligence results.

The report also acknowledges that with increased reporting volume and limited resources, the FIU faces challenges in providing detailed feedback on a case-by-case basis. Therefore, continuous improvement can be achieved through several methods: - Publishing information on crime types and emerging risks; - Publishing reports on negative examples; - Providing thematic guidance and regular quality feedback; - Conducting dialogues through public, private, or other channels. This feedback helps the agency adjust its investigation processes to achieve a more effective and intelligence-driven anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing framework. "Authorities, however, highlighted the practical challenges associated with providing detailed case-specific feedback, particularly in environments characterized by increasing reporting volumes and limited resources. Nevertheless, there was broad agreement that stronger feedback mechanisms, whether through negative typology publications, thematic guidance, public-private dialogue, or other channels, could play an important role in improving reporting effectiveness over time..." Summary: While the participants in this workshop did not reach a consensus on all issues, especially regarding the practical limits of tracing historical crypto-asset activity, there was broad consensus on principles such as appropriateness, explainability, cooperation, and intelligence-driven approaches to financial crime management. Submitting STR/SAR reports is not the end point, but rather the starting point for subsequent financial intelligence analysis, investigations, and actions. Their value should be judged by their contribution to the results of subsequent investigations and operations, not just by whether they are submitted. The ultimate goal is to improve the quality, value, and impact of reports, enabling them to provide meaningful intelligence and more effectively support the discovery, understanding, and combating of illicit financial activities. Original report link: https://baselgovernance.org/resources/publications/crypto-str-report/

data.title: Musk announced that he would give two shares of SpaceX stock to every child in the United States.
data.description:
"Two shares of stock, binding a generation. This isn't charity; it's putting the next generation directly on the shareholder list." On November 26, 2026, Musk posted several messages on SpaceX, announcing something that stunned the tech and financial worlds: every American child would receive two shares of SpaceX stock—one gifted by the company, and the other personally purchased by him. No threshold, no lottery, no first-come, first-served. Musk, who always likes to take things to extremes, has now directly bestowed the title of "shareholder for all" upon over 70 million American children. The biggest question after the announcement wasn't "whether they can get it," but rather—how exactly is this unprecedented stock grant arranged, and can it actually be fulfilled?

Stock Grant Details and Timeline

Musk only said one sentence in the original post, but it contained a great deal of information: Every child in the United States will receive two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from him personally. This post quickly garnered millions of views on SpaceX, with shares and likes skyrocketing.

— Musk Announces Stock Grant Plan on SpaceX

Two Shares, Received in Two Installments

In subsequent comments, Musk clarified the timeline: the shares provided by the company will be transferred next month, in December 2026; while his personally held shares will not be transferred until the lock-up period ends in June 2027.

Source of SharesTransfer Time
One share gifted by SpaceXDecember 2026
One share gifted personally by MuskJune 2027 (after the lock-up period ends)

This timeline reveals two things: the company's shares are readily available, while the personal shares are locked. In other words, the share truly embodying "Musk's personal commitment" is actually due next summer.

Linked to "Trump Accounts," Targeting the Next Generation

This share gift isn't simply putting shares into each child's hands; instead, it uses a pre-existing channel—"Trump Accounts." This is a tax-advantaged investment account set up by the US government for minors under the age of 18. The White House previously disclosed that nearly 70 million such accounts have been created, and more than 60 million children have been automatically registered.

—“Shareholders, start from childhood”

Musk is not the only one taking action on this path.

In July of this year, SpaceX President and Chief Operating Officer Gwen Shotwell announced that she would personally donate more than 2 million SpaceX shares to the next generation of Americans. The two, one after the other, brought the concept of "next-generation stock ownership" to the forefront. "He's not just giving away two shares; he's giving away tickets to put a generation on a rocket." Envisioning Multiplanetary Life At the same time as announcing the stock donation, Musk, as usual, threw out his grand, almost insane vision: if SpaceX successfully enables multiplanetary life and utilizes one millionth of the sun's energy, its value will be equivalent to a million times the current global economy.

— Musk and Starship Rockets

He himself admitted that these goals are "obviously absurdly difficult," but immediately followed up with—"There is a path to achieving them." This sentence is almost standard in all of Musk's grand narratives: first acknowledge the difficulty, then announce the path.

Interestingly, just one day before the stock-giving announcement, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) authorized a space data center plan, allowing up to 1 million satellites to serve AI computing power. It's no coincidence that space computing power and the multi-planetary narrative were placed on the same table in the same week.

— FCC Authorization Notice Regarding Space Data Center

Unprecedented Scale, Performance Under Scrutiny

There are approximately 73 million children under the age of 18 in the United States. Based on SpaceX's recent valuation of approximately $146 per share, Musk's personal donation alone is worth over $10 billion. Adding the company's share and the 2 million shares of Shotwell, this would be one of the largest single personal asset donations in human history.

Three unanswered questions

  1. Who is eligible? Qualifications, account management, and tax arrangements are currently not detailed.
  2. How is the valuation calculated?
    3. SpaceX is a privately held company, and its recent valuation of $146 per share lacks public market validation. Can the promise be fulfilled? Musk signed the Giving Pledge in 2012, and his foundation's past donation record has sparked discussions about potential "unpaid donations." On a more realistic level, SpaceX's stock price is not currently at an all-time high. Looking at the candlestick chart, the stock price has fallen steadily from its early October high, and was at a relatively low level when the stock grant announcement was made. This adds an extra layer of uncertainty to the "$146 per share" valuation assumption.

    — SpaceX Stock Price Daily K-line

    Therefore, it's too early to conclude which of the two directions this event will ultimately take: either it will become a landmark event symbolizing a generation sharing the benefits of space exploration, or it will slowly fade from public view amidst numerous questions surrounding details, valuation, and realization.

    Conclusion

    Musk's greatest strength has never been simply doing charity, but rather turning charity into a narrative. The two shares given away may not be the largest amount, but their symbolic significance is enough to go viral: every child who receives the shares becomes a node in the SpaceX story.

    He's used this strategy many times before—using Tesla to open up the electric vehicle market, using Starlink to expand the global network, and now using "universal shareholders" to tie SpaceX's future to the next generation. Whether this $10 billion will ultimately become a real number in 70 million accounts is anyone's guess. But at least on this day, everyone remembers one thing: he sold his space dream as the first asset for the next generation.
