**Detailed Explanation: The Possibility of Overturning 36 Crypto Policies from the Trump Era** **Author: jk; Editor: Hao Fangzhou** **Produced by: Odaily Planet Daily** **Introduction: How Many of the 36 Policies Can Be Overturned?** **Since Trump's return to the White House in January 2025, there has been a significant shift in US crypto regulation. Congress passed the first federal stablecoin law, the White House signed multiple executive orders related to digital assets, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) withdrew numerous lawsuits and successively introduced exemptions, interpretations, and rule proposals, and banking regulators withdrew their previous restrictive guidance on crypto businesses.** **However, in the November 2026 midterm elections, the Democrats won both the House of Representatives and the Senate. The new Congress will begin its term on January 3, 2027.** However, Trump's presidency extends to January 2029, giving him veto power, while the Democrats are still far from the two-thirds majority needed to override a veto (67 votes in the Senate and 290 votes in the House). This means that from 2027 to 2028, Democrats can block new encryption laws, launch investigations, and refuse to approve appointments, but they cannot repeal any measures already in effect. But once a Democratic president takes office in 2028, they can begin to overturn these decisions. A common assessment is that once the Democrats take over, everything enacted after the GENIUS Act could be overturned. This assessment is only partially true: whether a policy can be overturned depends not on its order of enactment, but on its legal form. In the past two years, there have been written laws passed by Congress, executive orders that the president can revoke with a single stroke, and statements from staff within regulatory agencies—the fragility of these three varies drastically. A measure that is legally easy to revoke does not necessarily mean it is easy to revoke in reality. ETFs already listed on the stock exchange, federal licenses already issued, and businesses built around the new rules by banks will become fait accompli, imposing high political and market costs on latecomers. This article systematically reviews the 36 major measures implemented during this period, explaining each one: what bill it is, who issued it, its current status, and how difficult it would be to overturn if the Democrats regain power. This article categorizes reversibility into four levels: "High" means that a new administration or new agency head can rescind it within a short period, typically represented by executive orders and agency guidelines. "Medium" means that the rule-making process needs to be restarted, usually taking one to two years, and may face legal challenges. "Low" means that Congress must pass new legislation to change it, which is almost impossible with the 60-vote threshold in the Senate. "Irreversible" means that matters such as pardons and concluded lawsuits are essentially irreversible from a legal perspective. The main text is arranged in descending order of reversibility.

I. High Reversibility: New government and Congress can rescind them in a short time (13 items)

This category contains 13 items, including executive orders, presidential task force reports, employee statements, explanatory letters, withdrawals of guidance, rules still in the proposal stage, and internal memos from the Department of Justice. They share the common characteristic of having a weak legal basis; a new government or new agency head can rescind, shelve, or rewrite them without congressional approval.

1. SEC Employee Statements and Guidance

Between 2025 and 2026, SEC staff issued a series of “employee statements” expressing their views on whether certain types of transactions or activities constitute securities.

The topics covered include Meme Coin, Proof-of-Work (PoW) mining, certain stablecoins, protocol staking, and liquidity staking. It also includes the broker-custodian statement from December 2025, the tokenized securities taxonomy from January 2026, and the stance on self-custodial interfaces from April 2026. These statements, not subject to committee votes, are not legally binding, but are effectively used as a "safe harbor" by the market, with the industry adjusting its operations accordingly. These statements are roughly chronologically as follows: February 27, 2025, Regarding Meme Coin: It states that their value is primarily driven by market demand and speculation, and that offerings do not require SEC registration, meaning they are not considered securities. March 20, 2025, Regarding Proof-of-Work (PoW) Mining: It states that mining on a PoW network does not constitute an offering or sale of securities, including self-mining. April 2025, Regarding "Covered Stablecoins": It was also considered that these stablecoins were not securities. May 29, 2025, Regarding Protocol Staking: It was determined that staking on a proof-of-stake network, whether done independently or through a third-party service, does not constitute a securities offering. At that time, liquidity staking and re-staking were not covered. The company's finance department later issued a separate statement confirming that liquidity staking and pledge tokens that meet the descriptions also do not constitute a securities offering. December 17, 2025, Regarding Brokerage Custody: It explained how brokerages meet the "actual possession" requirement of the Customer Protection Rule (Rule 15c3-3) for crypto asset securities. The practical approach is to control the corresponding private key and maintain on-chain transfer capabilities. January 28, 2026, Statement on Tokenized Securities: It reiterated that tokenized securities are still securities and categorized them into securities tokenized by the issuer itself and securities tokenized by a third party. The latter further distinguishes between custodial and synthetic securities.

On April 13, 2026, regarding “Covered User Interface”: As long as a website, browser plugin, or application does not host user assets, does not recommend specific transactions, and meets other conditions, staff will not recommend enforcement action against it for not being registered as a brokerage. This statement will automatically rescind after five years unless the Commission takes further action.

Reversibility is “High”. Non-binding means it can be rescinded overnight. This is something law firms repeatedly remind clients about the significant uncertainty involved in building business on employee statements.

2. SEC's Proposed Regulation of Crypto Assets

This is the SEC's most important crypto rule proposal to date, released on August 18, 2026.

It designs a specific set of fundraising and disclosure rules for crypto projects, including a $5 million startup phase exemption, two tiers of fundraising exemptions (tier one capped at $20 million, tier two at $75 million), a safe harbor system, and priority application of state laws. It allows a crypto project to legally issue tokens and raise funds under specific limits and conditions, without needing to register fully according to traditional securities offering standards. The comment period ends on October 20, 2026, and it has not yet been formally approved.

SEC's official statement, source: SEC website

Reversibility is currently "high" because it is currently only a proposal and can be declared invalid or rewritten.

Once finalized in 2027-2028, it will become "neutral," requiring a new rule-making process. If it's delayed until the final stage of Trump's term, around the end of 2028, it may fall into the CRA's retroactive window and be directly repealed by the new Congress. 3. CFTC's Crypto Asset Market Rules The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) is the agency that regulates the futures, options, and other derivatives markets. Its current situation is quite unique: Chairman Michael Selig was confirmed by the Senate on December 18, 2025, by a vote of 53 to 43, and former acting chairman Caroline Pham subsequently left to join MoonPay. Legally, the CFTC governs leveraged, margined, or retail-financed crypto commodity trading; for fully paid spot transactions, it can only handle fraud and manipulation. This "statutory ceiling" applies equally to both pro-crypto and future-oriented commissions. In this context, on September 17, 2026, the CFTC submitted a preliminary rule document entitled "Rules for Crypto-Asset Trading and Crypto-Asset Markets" (RIN 3038-AF80) to the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA). The text is now publicly available as an Advance Notice of Rulemaking (ANPRM), with a 60-day comment period following its publication in the Federal Register, which has now ended. The main content of this document defines the scope of crypto-asset regulation: it only applies to retail commodity transactions as defined in Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act, namely leveraged, margined, or financed retail crypto-asset transactions (CTX). These transactions must be conducted on designated contract markets (DCMs), unless otherwise specified. The document's definition of "crypto-asset" excludes payment-type stablecoins issued by issuers licensed under the GENIUS Act and provides preliminary explanations of what constitutes an "offer" and what constitutes "actual settlement."

Reversibility is "high". Measures in the pre-proposal stage are easily shelved when policies shift.

4. CFTC Employee Guidance and "No-Action Letter"

CFTC staff released frequently asked questions about crypto assets on March 20 and September 24, 2026, covering topics such as tokenized collateral and margin. Additionally, Employee Letter 26-25 made a "no-action" commitment regarding "passive software," meaning staff indicated that enforcement action would not be taken against such software providers under certain conditions.

The specific contents of these documents are as follows:

The December 2025 employee letter allows the use of real-world assets such as tokenized U.S. Treasury bonds and money market fund units as collateral; 26-05 is a "no-action" stance, allowing futures commission merchants (FCMs) to accept non-security digital assets such as Bitcoin, Ethereum, and payment stablecoins as margin for clients.

The letter dated March 20, 2026, supplemented the above-mentioned letter with operational details, stipulating that: crypto assets (including payment-type stablecoins) cannot be used as eligible collateral for non-liquidation swaps, but tokenized eligible collateral can be used as long as it is granted the same legal and economic rights; clearinghouses can accept crypto assets, including payment-type stablecoins, as initial collateral, provided that credit, market, and liquidity risk requirements are met. The employee letter dated March 17, 2026, gave wallet software developer Phantom Technologies a "no-action" position, exempting it from registering as an introducing broker. The same conditions were extended to all "passive software providers," i.e., wallets or applications that only provide a front-end that routes users to regulated futures commission merchants, introducing brokers, and designated contract markets. Reversibility is "high." Employee guidance and no-action letters can be revoked by staff or a new committee. 5. Specific Implementation Details of GENIUS (from the Treasury Department, FDIC, NCUA, and FinCEN) The implementation of the GENIUS Act requires the involvement of numerous government agencies: the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), the Treasury Department, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA), and the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) are each responsible for specific details, covering deposit insurance, credit unions issuing stablecoins, anti-money laundering obligations, and more. As of November 2026, approximately 13 rules are still in the proposal stage. Among them, the Treasury Department's interim final rule regarding the certification process for state-level regulatory systems took effect on September 30, 2026; the "substantially similar" state-level regulatory principle proposed by the Treasury Department in April 2026 has not yet been finalized. "Substantially similar" means that if a state government's stablecoin regulatory system is substantially similar to federal standards, its issuer can pursue a state-level path. Reversibility is "high" in terms of "content". Rules proposed during the drafting phase can be rewritten by the new leadership or finalized in different directions. However, the legally mandated legislation will not disappear; the new government must complete the rules within the legal framework, and cannot leave them in limbo. 6. Executive Order 14178: "Strengthening U.S. Leadership in Digital Financial Technology" (CBDC Prohibition) This is the first major crypto executive order signed by Trump after returning to the White House, dated January 23, 2025. Its functions are threefold: declaring federal government support for the development of the digital asset industry, prohibiting federal agencies from promoting central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), and establishing the "President's Working Group on Digital Asset Markets" (PWG), which will be responsible for proposing regulatory framework recommendations.

Original text of the bill, source: White House website

The CBDC ban mentioned in Section 34 currently relies solely on this order at the federal level.

Reversibility is "high". The next president can rescind it on their first day in office. The CBDC ban will only become secure after Congress passes separate legislation.

7. Executive Order 14331: "Ensuring fair access to banking services for all Americans" (anti-"debanking")

"Debanking" refers to banks refusing to provide account services to specific individuals or businesses for reasons other than financial risk, such as political stance or industry reputation.

During the Biden administration, the crypto industry has long complained of being the primary victim. This order, signed on August 7, 2025, requires federal banking regulators to clean up related practices. The order itself doesn't create any rights that can be asserted in court; the real binding force comes from the subsequent final rules issued by the OCC and FDIC (see Item 23). The crypto industry's narrative is that during the Biden administration, there was an "Operation Choke Point 2.0" targeting the industry. This name, coined by crypto venture capitalist Nic Carter, stemmed from the collapse of three crypto-friendly U.S. banks, which he viewed as a "conspiracy" aimed at preventing crypto companies from accessing banking services. While this accusation remains controversial, it became central to the Trump campaign's narrative: at the White House Crypto Summit in March 2025, Trump announced the end of this operation; this executive order requires a retrospective review of past complaints and banking regulatory records. The text of the order doesn't explicitly name "crypto," but it prohibits the "politicization or illegal debanking" of any legitimate business, extending its protection beyond the crypto industry.

Regarding the order itself, reversibility is "high".

8. Executive Order 14405: "Integrating Fintech Innovation into the Regulatory Framework"

This order, issued on May 19, 2026, requires financial regulatory agencies to review their rules within 90-day and 180-day periods, removing obstacles hindering fintech and crypto businesses, and requires the Federal Reserve to submit a report on fintech companies' access to payment accounts. It is a continuation of the aforementioned executive orders, shifting the focus from "statements" to "institutional-by-institutional rule cleanup".

Reversibility is "high," meaning the next president can rescind it on their first day in office.

9. Interpretive Letter from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)

An "interpretive letter" is a formal response from the OCC regarding what banks "can do".

These letters, issued in 2025, clarified that banks can provide crypto asset custody, participate in stablecoin business, operate blockchain nodes, and hold crypto assets to pay network fees. The specific contents of the three letters are as follows: Letter 1183 confirms the feasibility of participating in distributed ledger activities such as independent node verification networks. It also rescinds Letter 1179, which required banks to obtain a "no objection" opinion from regulators before engaging in these activities. Letter 1184 allows banks to buy and sell assets in custody according to customer instructions and to outsource custody-related services permitted by the bank itself to third parties. Letter 1186 confirms that National Bank can pay blockchain network fees (i.e., gas fees) to conduct already permitted business and can also hold crypto assets to test already permitted crypto platforms.

Original text of the explanatory letter, source: OCC official website

Reversibility is "high". The new OCC head can directly revoke these letters. Such revocations have occurred before, for example, Explanatory Letter 1179 issued in 2021 was revoked by Letter 1183 in 2025 after the Trump administration took office.

10. FDIC and Federal Reserve Guidance

FDIC's FIL-7-2025, issued in 2025, eliminated the requirement for banks to notify regulators in advance before conducting crypto-related business.

On April 24, 2025, the Federal Reserve withdrew its previous regulatory guidance on crypto assets; on August 15, 2025, it also ended the "New Activities Surveillance Program" and Regulatory Letter SR 23-7, both of which were previously the Fed's main tools for reviewing banks' crypto businesses. Reversibility is "high". New guidance can be directly reissued without public comment. 11. Fed "Payment Account" ("Slimmed-down Master Account") The master account is an account opened by an institution with the Federal Reserve. With it, the institution can directly access the Fed's payment and clearing system without having to go through a partner bank. Crypto companies and fintech companies have long considered this a key bottleneck. In March 2026, Kraken received a 12-month limited master account pilot program; on May 20, 2026, the Federal Reserve proposed the "Payment Account" (Docket OP-1878) proposal, opening up a more restrictive, less privileged "slimmed-down" account to fintech and crypto companies. The comment period ended on July 27, 2026, and the proposal is still pending; decisions for some Tier 3 applicants have been suspended until the end of the year. Reversibility is rated "high" before the finalization. The outcome depends more on the composition of the Federal Reserve Board than on the 2028 presidential election. 12. Department of Justice Memorandum on "Ending Regulation by Prosecution" On April 7, 2025, Deputy Attorney General Blanche issued an internal memorandum entitled "Ending Regulation by Prosecution," disbanding the National Cryptocurrency Enforcement Team (NCET), which was specifically responsible for crypto cases. Its position is that prosecutors should not use criminal prosecutions to enforce rules that belong to regulatory agencies. This is internal policy, not law. Reversibility is "high" for the future; a new Attorney General can directly rescind the decision. However, cases that have exceeded the statute of limitations or have been abandoned are difficult to re-investigate. 13. Presidential Working Group on Digital Assets Report (Legislative Reference) The Presidential Working Group on Digital Asset Markets released a report on the digital asset market in July 2025, proposing policy recommendations covering multiple areas including stablecoins, market structure, taxation, and banking. This report itself is not binding; it is neither law nor rule, but it provides a policy basis for a series of subsequent regulatory actions, and some of its recommendations have already been adopted by various agencies. Reversibility is "high." Because it has no legal effect, the next government can completely disregard it or start anew.

II. Legally Easy to Revoke, but Faces Real-World Obstacles (Items 14-16)

These three items can also be revoked relatively quickly legally, but subsequent rules, existing assets, or the established business of banks make the actual cost of revocation significantly higher than the difficulties on paper.

14. Executive Order 14330: Including Alternative Assets (Including Crypto Assets) in 401(k) Retirement Accounts

401(k) is the most prevalent employer-sponsored retirement plan in the United States, with tens of millions of Americans enrolling their retirement savings in it. This order, also signed on August 7, 2025, requires the Department of Labor (DOL) to review the rules to make alternative assets, including crypto assets, more easily accessible as investment options in retirement accounts. The DOL released a rule proposal on March 30, 2026, and the final rule was submitted to the White House's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) for review in November 2026. This office is responsible for the final administrative review before the rule is officially released.

Once the final rule is published, overturning it requires going through the rulemaking process again, which is of medium difficulty. Furthermore, if this rule is not finalized until around the end of 2028, it may fall into the "retroactive window" of congressional review and be repealed by the new Congress using the CRA.

15. Executive Order 14233: Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and Digital Asset Stockpile

This order, signed on March 6, 2025, announces the establishment of a "Strategic Bitcoin Reserve" and a "Digital Asset Stockpile."

The core idea is to centralize the Bitcoins acquired by the federal government through criminal or civil forfeiture, hold them as a long-term national reserve, and not sell them arbitrarily. To date, the government has not announced any plans to purchase them on the open market. According to estimates by BitcoinTreasuries, the government holds approximately 328,372 Bitcoins. There are also reports of a dispute between the Treasury Department and the Commerce Department regarding who should hold the reserve.

The reserves currently exist solely on this order, without any legal protection. Legally, reversibility is "high," meaning the next president could rescind it on day one and resume the sale of confiscated Bitcoin; practically, it's "medium," as asset forfeiture procedures and compensation arrangements for victims limit the government's ability to arbitrarily sell these coins. 16. SEC Reverses SAB 121 (Replacing it with SAB 122) SAB is the SEC's "Staff Accounting Bulletin." SAB 121 in 2022 required companies that custodied crypto assets for clients to list these assets as liabilities on their balance sheets, making it virtually impossible for banks to offer crypto custody services. In January 2025, the SEC reversed it through SAB 122. It's important to clarify that this is an employee-level reversal, not a congressional CRA process; Congress passed a resolution to overturn SAB 121 in 2024, but it was vetoed by Biden.

SEC's employee accounting announcement, source: SEC website

Legally, employee announcements can be reissued by the SEC later. However, in reality, banks have already built products and teams around custody services, making retraction difficult in practice. The reversibility in practice is not high.

III. Reversibility (Items 17 to 24)

This category requires the regulatory agency to make a formal new decision, but it does not necessarily require going through the complete rule-making process again. Therefore, it is slower than the first category, but still relatively easier.

17. The SEC and CFTC's "Joint Interpretation" and Token Taxonomy

On March 17, 2026, the SEC and CFTC jointly released a committee-level interpretative document classifying crypto assets into five categories: digital goods, collectibles, instruments, stablecoins, and digital securities. This was an attempt to provide a temporary answer to "which tokens belong to the SEC and which belong to the CFTC" in the absence of congressional legislation. It holds a higher rank than employee statements because it was voted on by the committee.

An interpretative document can be withdrawn without public comment, but market participants have already shaped their businesses accordingly, and a sudden reversal could invite legal challenges of "arbitrary" decisions.

18. SEC's "Innovation Exemption": On-Chain Trading of Tokenized Stocks

On September 17, 2026, the SEC granted a five-year conditional exemption (Release 34-106402) for "tokenized National Market System stocks." Tokenized stocks refer to securities represented by blockchain tokens and linked to the stock of real-world listed companies. The exemption allows these products to be traded on-chain. The exemption is valid until September 17, 2031, but includes a "modifiable" clause. Chairman Atkins himself stated that this exemption "must be followed by the development of lasting rules."

The Commission can modify or terminate the exemption with a new order without having to go through the full rulemaking process again.

19. OCC's Issuance of National Trust Bank Licenses to Crypto Companies

A national trust bank license is a federal-level license. Licensed institutions can provide custody and stablecoin-related services nationwide, without needing to apply for licenses state by state. The OCC has approved a batch of applications since December 2025. Final approvals were granted to Ripple (October 2026), Circle, BitGo, and Coinbase (November 2026); conditional approvals were granted to Paxos, Fidelity Digital Assets, Crypto.com, Bridge, Protego, and World Liberty Trust (an entity under World Liberty Financial, related to the Trump family) in August 2026. In October 2026, the Independent Community Banking Association (ICBA) filed a lawsuit challenging the OCC's authority to issue such licenses to crypto companies.

Reversibility needs to be considered in two ways. The reversibility of licenses that have already been finalized is low because revocation requires a legitimate reason.

Conditional approvals can be delayed or denied final confirmation. Democratic lawmakers have made it clear they will investigate the OCC's conditional approval of World Liberty Trust. 20. GENIUS Implementation Rules of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (12 CFR Part 15) The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) is the agency that regulates federally registered banks and is one of the main enforcers of the GENIUS Act. The OCC issued its final rule on October 21, 2026, published on October 23, totaling 721 pages, and added Part 15 of Title 12 of the Compilation of Federal Regulations. The rule specifies stress test and liquidity buffer requirements for issuers, sets a minimum capital requirement of $5 million, allows short-term Treasury repurchase transactions with prior approval, and establishes an exemption process for issuers who have submitted applications before January 18, 2027. The preamble states that the OCC has anti-circumvention authority over actions that circumvent yield restrictions. The rule will also take effect on January 18, 2027. The final rule must be amended through the new rulemaking process, which requires public comment and a reasonable explanation, typically taking one to two years. However, the OCC's comptroller is appointed by the president and can be dismissed at any time. Therefore, if the Democrats come to power in 2029, they can tighten requirements through new rules within the bounds of the law. 21. Ending Investigations into Robinhood Crypto, Uniswap Labs, OpenSea, etc. In 2025, the SEC also closed investigations into a number of companies without taking enforcement action, including Robinhood Crypto, Uniswap Labs, Crypto.com, OpenSea, Yuga Labs, and Gemini. Investigations are different from lawsuits; they are merely internal investigation procedures within regulatory agencies, and "closing" does not mean a legal conclusion. Theoretically, the new SEC could reopen investigations within the statute of limitations for fines (five years, according to the report). However, in reality, evidence collection is costly and opportunities may have passed, making restarts rare. 22. Universal Listing Standards for ETFs Previously, each cryptocurrency ETF required individual SEC approval, a lengthy and uncertain process. On September 17, 2025, the SEC approved rule changes for Nasdaq, Cboe BZX, and NYSE Arca, establishing "universal listing standards." Eligible commodity trust units (including crypto assets) can now be listed without individual approval. This change significantly reduces the time to market for new products. The future SEC can require exchanges to modify standards or re-examine them under the powers of Section 19 of the Securities Exchange Act, but removing already listed products from the market is another matter (see Item 27).

23. OCC and FDIC's "Reputation Risk" Rules

"Reputation risk" is a vague concept that regulators used in the past, which they could use to suggest that banks should not serve certain types of customers. Crypto companies were a major victim of this. On April 7, 2026, the OCC and FDIC issued a final rule removing this concept from the regulatory system and prohibiting regulator-driven debanking. The rule took effect on June 9, 2026. Another final rule regarding "unsafe or unsound practices" was issued in August of the same year. This is the implementation version of Executive Order 7.

Joint statement from the OCC and FDIC, source: FDIC official website

Revoking it would require going through a new rulemaking process, which typically takes 12 to 24 months and could face court challenges under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). Because Trump holds a veto, the Democratic-controlled Congress cannot repeal it through the CRA before 2029.

24. Treasury Department OFAC lifts sanctions on Tornado Cash

Tornado Cash is a mixing protocol on Ethereum that allows users to "launder" the origin of their funds.

In 2022, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) of the Treasury Department added its smart contract address to the sanctions list, sparking questions from industry and the legal community. In March 2025, OFAC removed it from the sanctions list. Theoretically, OFAC could reinstate it, but the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals' ruling in the Van Loon case regarding "immutable smart contracts" limited its ability to do so.

IV. Low or Irreversible Reversibility (Items 25-32)

This category is either deeply embedded in the institution's daily operations or enshrined in law; overturning it would incur high political and market costs.

25. ETF Physical Redemption Mechanism

On July 29, 2025, the SEC approved "physical redemption" for Bitcoin and Ethereum exchange-traded products. Previously, authorized participants could only exchange or redeem ETF units with cash; now they can do so directly with Bitcoin and Ethereum, reducing operating costs and tax friction. This mechanism is already deeply embedded in the daily operations of fund companies, and forcibly reverting to it would incur significant operating costs. 26. GENIUS Act (Stablecoin Act) The GENIUS Act, Public Law 119-27, is the first federal law in the United States specifically regulating stablecoins. Signed by Trump on July 18, 2025, it defines stablecoins as cryptocurrencies whose value is pegged to fiat currencies such as the US dollar. USDT and USDC are the most common examples. The core idea of ​​the act is to establish a federal-level licensing and regulatory framework for stablecoin issuers, requiring issuers to hold sufficient high-quality reserve assets and restricting direct payments of yield to holders—the so-called "yield ban." This law has a broad political foundation. The Senate passed the bill 68-30, with 18 Democrats voting in favor; the House passed it 308-122, with 206 Republicans and 102 Democrats voting in favor. The bill stipulates that the effective date will be the earlier of two dates: 18 months after enactment, or 120 days after the release of final implementing rules. According to the legal timeline, regulatory agencies should have finalized their rules by July 18, 2026, a deadline that has already passed. Because the 18-month catch-up period has arrived earlier, the bill will take effect on January 18, 2027.

To amend this law, new legislation is required, and Trump holds veto power until January 2029. After that, even if the Democrats hold a complete majority in government, the bill will face the 60-vote threshold in the Senate. A more realistic path is to amend it, such as adding ethical rules for officials holding crypto assets, or closing loopholes to circumvent the yield ban, rather than repealing it entirely.

27. Listed Spot Crypto Asset ETFs

From October 2025 to the present, a number of spot crypto asset ETFs have been listed in the US market, including SOL (including staking ETFs such as BSOL), XRP, LTC, HBAR, DOGE, LINK, and the multi-asset product GDLC. According to Morgan Stanley data, there are approximately 140 cryptocurrency-related ETFs listed in the US, of which about 40 are single-asset spot products.

Forcing the delisting of products already held by investors would be an extremely rare move with significant political costs.

28. Congressional Review Bill Overturns IRS's DeFi Broker Rule (H.J.Res. 25)

This is the most solid victory of the entire period.

Towards the end of the Biden administration's term, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) issued a rule requiring certain participants in the decentralized finance (DeFi) sector to report user transaction information to the tax authorities as "brokers." The industry argued that decentralized protocols do not possess user identities and cannot fulfill this obligation, effectively banning DeFi. The tool Congress used to overturn this rule is the Congressional Review Act (CRA). This law stipulates that Congress can pass a resolution of "disapproval" by a simple majority within a certain period after the rule's issuance. Once signed by the president, the rule is void, and the agency cannot issue a "substantially similar" rule in the future unless otherwise authorized by Congress. H.J.Res. 25 was signed by Trump on April 10, 2025, becoming Public Law 119-5. It passed the Senate 70-28 and the House 292-132, with significant Democratic support. The Treasury Department removed the rule from the compilation of federal regulations on July 11, 2025. It's important to note that the 1099-DA reporting system for custodial brokers, implemented from the 2025 tax year, has not been repealed. Reversibility: It cannot be reversed without new legislation. After this rule was repealed by the CRA, no government can issue a substantially similar rule; Congress must legislate a new one. 29. Pardons Ross Ulbricht, BitMEX Founders, and CZ In 2025, Trump pardoned several iconic figures in the crypto industry, including Ross Ulbricht, sentenced to life imprisonment for operating the darknet marketplace Silk Road; the founding team of the crypto derivatives exchange BitMEX; and Binance founder CZ. The power of pardon is an independent power granted to the president by the Constitution and does not require congressional or court approval. Once a pardon is delivered, no successor can revoke it; this is the most thorough of the 36 measures.

30. Lawsuits Dropped Against Coinbase, Kraken, Consensys, Binance, etc.

Between February and May 2025, the SEC successively dropped previous lawsuits against several crypto companies, including Coinbase, Kraken, Consensys, Cumberland DRW, Dragonchain, Balina, and Binance. The core allegations in these lawsuits were that these companies provided securities trading, brokerage, or staking services without registration. According to the research report, these cases were dropped with "substantive effect," meaning that legally, the same lawsuits cannot be re-filed on the same issues.

A drop with substantive effect is legally known as res judicata, meaning that the case cannot be re-filed even if the commission changes.

31. Ripple Case Concluded

The SEC sued Ripple in 2020, alleging that the sale of XRP constituted an unregistered securities offering, becoming one of the most influential lawsuits in the crypto industry. In August 2025, both parties withdrew their appeals. The $125 million fine imposed by the district court remained unchanged, and the court did not approve the parties' proposed reduction of the fine to $50 million.

Reversibility was determined to be "irreversible," making this a final ruling.

32. Settlement between Justin Sun, Tron, and the SEC

On March 5, 2026, the SEC reached a settlement with Tron founder Justin Sun and related parties. Rainberry Inc. paid $10 million, and the charges against Sun and related foundations were withdrawn with substantive effect. This is another major legacy case resolved by the SEC in 2026.

Reversibility is "irreversible," meaning settlements and withdrawals with substantive effect are final outcomes.

V. Appendix: Bills Not Yet Law (Items 33-36)

These four items don't have the issue of "overthrowing," only "passing." In a new Congress controlled by the Democrats, they are unlikely to be passed.

33. CLARITY Act (Market Structure Act)

The CLARITY Act attempts to address the core legal issues in the crypto industry: which tokens are securities and governed by the SEC, which are commodities and governed by the CFTC, and how trading platforms, brokers, and custodians should be registered and regulated. It complements the GENIUS Act, which governs stablecoins, while CLARITY governs the structure of the entire trading market.

The House of Representatives passed the bill on July 17, 2025, by a vote of 294 to 134, with 216 Republicans and 78 Democrats in favor. In the Senate, the Agriculture Committee passed its version (the Digital Goods Intermediaries Act) by a vote of 12 to 11 on January 29, 2026, and the Banking Committee passed its report by a vote of 15 to 9 on May 14, 2026, with two Democrats in support. However, on September 15, 2026, the Senate voted 49 to 50 to end debate on the motion to proceed with the bill, falling short of the 60-vote threshold, with all Democrats and four Republicans voting against it. According to the law firm Orrick, the main disagreements centered on ethical rules regarding officials holding crypto assets and the issue of stablecoin yields. Senator Tillis's motion for reconsideration kept the bill alive during the recess, but law firms such as DLA Piper, Troutman Pepper Locke, and Orrick believe it has little chance of passing in this Congress. Because CLARITY is not law, it cannot be "overthrown." A newly elected Democratic-controlled Congress can effectively veto it simply by not pushing it forward. Troutman Pepper Locke also points out that regulators cannot replicate several core elements of this bill through rules, including the CFTC's licensing of spot intermediaries, priority protection of client assets in bankruptcy, and broad priority application of state laws. 34. Anti-CBDC Surveillance State Act Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) is a digital form of fiat currency issued directly by a central bank. There is strong opposition within the United States, with concerns that it would allow the government to monitor personal spending. This act, H.R. 1919, aims to prohibit the Federal Reserve from issuing CBDCs for retail users. The House of Representatives passed the bill on July 17, 2025, by a vote of 219 to 210; on April 29, 2026, this content was attached to the House amendment to S. 1318, but the Senate failed to reach a consensus, and the bill has not yet become law. Therefore, the only effective federal-level ban on CBDCs in the United States is currently Executive Order 14178 of January 2025 (see Item 6), which can be revoked by the next president. Unless Congress actually legislates, the stability of this ban is limited. 35. Digital Asset Tax Certainty Act This bill (H.R. 10357) is a long-awaited tax reform for crypto assets. It includes several provisions: setting a tax-free threshold for small transactions (the report refers to a $10 gas fee exemption), extending the "wash sale rule" applicable to stocks to crypto assets, and clarifying how staking and mining rewards are taxed. The so-called wash sale rule refers to the rule that if an investor sells an asset at a loss and then buys it back within 30 days, the loss cannot be used to offset taxes. Currently, crypto assets are not subject to this rule, and including them would close a tax loophole, but it is also a trade-off for the industry. The House Ways and Means Committee passed the bill 38-5 on September 16, 2026, but neither house voted on it. The attitude of Ron Wyden, who is expected to chair the Senate Finance Committee, will determine whether it can proceed during the recess. 36. The Bitcoin Act and the American Reserve Modernization Act (ARMA) The Bitcoin Act (S. 954), introduced by Senator Lummis, proposes that the federal government purchase large amounts of Bitcoin over several years as a national strategic reserve. The American Reserve Modernization Act (ARMA), another proposal related to reserve assets, passed the House Financial Services Committee 28-21 on September 16, 2026. Neither has become law. With the Democrats controlling Congress, such legislation is virtually impossible to pass. Relatedly, the current "strategic Bitcoin reserve" exists solely on an executive order (see item 15), lacking any legal basis.

Appendix: Five Types of Institutions and Legal Instruments

Background 1: How the US Congress Legislates

In the United States, for a bill to become law, it must first obtain a majority vote in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, and then be signed into law by the President. The Senate has a special threshold: a majority bill requires 60 votes to end debate and proceed to a vote; this process is called "cloture." Understanding these two points helps explain why legislation, once enacted by Congress, is difficult to repeal, and why some bills remain stuck in the Senate for extended periods.

Background 2: Executive Orders and Pardons

An executive order (EO) is a directive issued by the US President to the federal executive branch. It does not require congressional approval and takes effect very quickly.

Its advantage is flexibility, but its disadvantages are equally obvious: the next president can sign a new order that completely revoks it, so executive orders almost always rank first in terms of reversibility. Pardons, on the other hand, stem from a constitutional privilege granted to the president; once effective, there is almost no mechanism to reverse them. Background 3: What is the SEC and how does it operate now? The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is an independent federal agency regulating the securities market. Its most controversial practice in recent years was using litigation rather than rules to define which crypto assets are securities under former Chairman Gensler—a practice the industry calls "regulation through enforcement." Since current Chairman Paul Atkins took office, there has been a clear shift within the agency. Currently, there are no Democratic members on the commission (they are in the process of being nominated), and after Peirce announced his resignation on September 25, 2026, the commission will consist of only Chairman Atkins and Commissioner Uyeda. Background 4: OCC, FDIC, and the Federal Reserve For crypto companies to integrate with the traditional financial system, they cannot bypass three agencies: the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), which regulates federally registered banks; the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), which insures deposits; and the Federal Reserve. During the Biden administration, these three agencies acted as a "firewall" between banks and crypto businesses through a series of informal guidelines; the Trump administration, conversely, gradually dismantled these restrictions. Background 5: The Legal Authority and Current Situation of the SEC and CFTC After the CLARITY Act failed in the Senate, regulatory agencies began filling the gaps with their existing authority. A common characteristic of these measures is that most remain at the proposal, exemption, or internal guidance stage, with a much weaker legal basis than codified law. The law firm Troutman Pepper Locke commented that the actions of regulatory agencies "cannot provide certainty" and are "easily overturned" under future administrations. Another real-world context is that both agencies currently have extremely homogeneous compositions: the SEC has no Democratic commissioners, and the CFTC, since December 2025, has only had Chairman Michael Selig, and is currently nominating new commissioners. The Supreme Court overturned a century-old precedent in Trump v. Slaughter in June 2026, allowing the president to dismiss the head of an independent agency at any time, meaning the next president could take over these agencies very quickly. **Democracy Takeover Scenario Analysis and Final Conclusion** **Phase One:** Democrats Control Both Houses, Trump Remains in Office (January 2027 to January 2029) This is the current reality. The biggest tool the Democrats have in their hands during these two years is oversight power. It is expected that Elizabeth Warren will take over the Senate Banking Committee, Maxine Waters will take over the House Financial Services Committee, Robert Garcia will take over the House Oversight Committee, and there are also reports that Sherrod Brown will chair the Senate Agriculture Committee. They all indicated they would investigate World Liberty Financial, the USD1 stablecoin, $TRUMP Meme, and the OCC's conditional license approval for World Liberty Trust. Democrats could also shelve the CLARITY Act, Bitcoin reserve-related legislation, and crypto tax legislation. The Senate could refuse to confirm the SEC and CFTC nominees. SEC Chairman Atkins' term expires in June 2026, and the SEC website states that commissioners can continue serving for up to 18 months after their term ends, roughly the end of 2027 for Atkins. A Democratic Senate could keep both agencies understaffed, making their rules more legally challenging. What Democrats cannot do is equally clear. They cannot repeal the GENIUS Act, cannot use the CRA to overturn Trump administration rules (the president would veto it), and cannot rescind executive orders or reopen dismissed cases. Agencies can proceed with Trump's crypto agenda as per their existing mandates. Among the possible bipartisan consensuses, the most realistic is a smaller market structure bill with strict provisions for disclosure and divestiture of crypto assets by officials, and partial amendments to the GENIUS Act, such as closing yield loopholes. TD Cowen analyst Jaret Seiberg warns, however, that the current political climate may make an industry-acceptable CLARITY version "simply impossible to move forward." **Phase Two:** Democrats gain complete control after the 2028 election (starting January 2029) **Once the Democrats control both the White House and Congress, things will proceed in three phases. On the first day, they can rescind Executive Orders 14178, 14233, 14330, 14331, and 14405, withdraw the Justice Department memorandum, and replace the leadership of the SEC and CFTC. On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court overturned Humphrey's Executor precedent in Trump v. Slaughter by a 6-3 decision, allowing the president to dismiss commissioners of independent agencies with minimal obstacles, although the statutory limit of no more than three seats per party remains. Within months, employee declarations, OCC interpretative letters, and letters of no action can be withdrawn, innovation exemptions can be modified or terminated, and pending proposals can be rewritten or torn up. Within one to two years, new rulemaking will be needed to dismantle reputational risk rules, finalized crypto asset rules, and Department of Labor rules, and to tighten the enforcement of the GENIUS Act, including provisions on reserves, capital, earnings anti-circumvention, and state certification. Meanwhile, according to the Congressional Research Service, rules submitted to Congress within a certain period before the end of the previous congressional session (less than 60 days in the Senate or 60 days in the House of Representatives) can be reviewed by the new Congress using the CRA. This means that if Regulation Crypto Assets, the CFTC's crypto rules, or the Department of Labor's 401(k) rules are not finalized by the end of 2028, they risk being repealed with a single click. Even in this scenario, several things are highly unlikely: the complete repeal of the GENIUS Act (requiring 60 Senate votes, many of whom are co-voters), the revocation of pardons, the reopening of dismissed cases, and the forced delisting of already listed ETFs.

data.title: Who is pricing Stripe at $200 billion?
data.description:
The combined market capitalization of PayPal, Block, Adyen, and Fiserv is still about one PayPal short of being equal to Stripe's.

On November 24th, the Wall Street Journal reported that Stripe is negotiating a new round of employee stock offers with investors, with a valuation expected to exceed $200 billion, and a deal could be finalized as early as the beginning of next year.

The last offer was made in February of this year. Investors such as Thrive, Coatue, and a16z bought employee stock, and Stripe also repurchased it with cash, at which time the valuation was $159 billion.

A few months later, Stripe positioned itself as "AI economic infrastructure" at the conference and completed its acquisition of the model routing platform OpenRouter. So how should we value this fastest-growing financial unicorn in the world today? Or has it transcended the definition of a payment company? I. Employees Sell Stock, Existing Shareholders Increase Holdings, Stripe Pays. In 2023, Stripe encountered a very real problem. Employees received stock-based awards, but the related withheld taxes had to be paid in cash. Stripe then raised over $6.5 billion at a valuation of $50 billion, arranging for current and former employees to cash out and handle taxes, and then using the cancelled shares to offset shares issued to new investors. The company specifically stated in its announcement that this money was not needed for daily operations. Starting in 2024, employees will have a window to sell shares almost every year. Buyers pay the selling employee the offer price, and the outside world uses this price per share to estimate Stripe's value. Business Model Analyst categorizes the uses of this price into four aspects. The first two are easy to understand: employees know how much cash they can get when selling their shares; existing shareholders also know the approximate value of their remaining shares. The other two issues fell on Stripe itself. In February, the majority of the money for buying employee stock came from investors, with Stripe also contributing cash. The higher the stock price, the fewer shares could be bought back with the same amount of money. In August, Stripe signed an agreement to acquire OpenRouter, reportedly with the consideration primarily in stock, according to Axios. This time, the tables were reversed: as long as the seller accepted a higher price per share for the same company, Stripe could offer fewer shares. Employees have the opportunity to cash out a portion of their shares annually, and Stripe also has funds for buybacks and investment in new businesses. In the first half of this year, the company's free cash flow increased by 43% year-on-year. Several things that could have been resolved by going public have already been accomplished in the private market. According to the Wall Street Journal, Stripe executives believe that the uncertainty brought about by AI makes remaining private more advantageous for the company. II. From $91.5 billion to $159 billion, and then to $200 billion. [Image of Stripe valuation comparison chart] Periodic tender offers provided employees with opportunities to sell shares and also gave us a benchmark. The 2024 tender offer corresponded to a valuation of $65 billion. Over the next two years, buyers offered increasingly higher prices: how much of this was due to Stripe's increased revenue, and how much was because buyers were willing to pay more for the same dollar of revenue? The employee stock offer in February 2025 valued Stripe at $91.5 billion. Based on 2024 net revenue of approximately $5.1 billion, the price-to-sales ratio was about 18. A year later, a new offer raised the valuation to $159 billion. Based on 2025 net revenue of approximately $6.8 billion to $6.9 billion, the price buyers were offering for each dollar of net revenue rose from about $18 to about $23. If investors continued to offer at the original 18x multiple, Stripe's valuation would likely reach approximately $123 billion once its revenue grew significantly. In total, the increase from $91.5 billion to $159 billion was roughly half due to revenue growth and the other half due to exponential increases. Even Thrive, which participated in the tender offer, had already specifically expressed optimism about stablecoins and Agentic Commerce at the time. Both tender offers occurred in February, which is a good time to read the Collison brothers' annual report. Let's first see how they described this business then, and then see where they spent their money later. 2.1 Programmable Financial Services The letter from February 2025 focused primarily on how merchants could collect payments. A slightly higher payment success rate meant existing customers could make more business, and merchants from other providers would have another reason to switch to Stripe. At that time, the software suite centered around Billing had already achieved annualized revenue exceeding $500 million, but when the Collison brothers discussed growth, they still prioritized the investments in payment products over the past few years. At the Stripe Sessions that same year, management used "programmable financial services" to summarize the business Stripe was building. AI and stablecoins were listed as two driving forces for business growth over the next decade. At the time, the most clearly visible AI products were payment infrastructure models: identifying fraud, optimizing payments, and enabling more transactions for the same group of merchants to succeed. AI primarily improved the economic efficiency of the core payment business. A year later, the Collison brothers devoted considerable space in their letter to their newly launched clients. Some companies generated substantial revenue within months, and AI companies were particularly successful in selling overseas on day one. Things that merchants used to only inquire about when they grew large—how to receive foreign currency, how to pay taxes in different markets, how to bill based on usage—were now addressed from the outset. For the buyers in that $159 billion round, these smaller companies were worth considering. The sooner Stripe secures its first business deal, the more likely it is to profit alongside those established companies as they grow. This context is reflected in the letter's discussions of Metronome, stablecoins, and agent commerce. At the April 2026 Sessions, Patrick Collison stated the conference's theme directly at the outset: Stripe is building "the economic infrastructure for the AI ​​era." This statement simultaneously addresses two types of customer needs: AI companies need to charge customers based on usage, and shopping agents need to make payments on behalf of users after obtaining authorization. The former has already been handled by Billing and Metronome, while the latter has Link's agent wallet; the scale of transactions it can generate remains to be seen.

2.3 Token Model and Bill

In August, Stripe announced the acquisition of OpenRouter and wrote a separate letter to investors. Why would a payment company manage model calls? From the developer's perspective, it's easy to understand: how much the customer pays is recorded as revenue, and the money spent on the backend to call the model is recorded as cost. To know whether this deal was profitable, the accounts on both sides need to be reconciled sooner or later. Management also disclosed that first-half billing increased by 71% year-on-year, stating that the profitability of the core payment business supported these acquisitions. The former refers to existing operating performance at the time; whether OpenRouter could generate sufficient new profits remained to be seen. On the same day, the OpenRouter founding team also wrote an open letter to developers explaining why they accepted the deal. They pledged to maintain the neutrality of multi-model selection and routing, and valued Stripe's merchant network and risk control capabilities. OpenRouter was one of these acquisitions. The acquisition of Metronome earlier this year allowed Stripe to charge merchants based on usage; Clerky pushed its outreach to entrepreneurs back to company establishment; and in September, Stripe signed an agreement to acquire Parafin, extending its business to when platform merchants needed funding. The four transactions spanned several stages of a company's development: its initial establishment, the start of charging fees, calculating model costs, and the need for working capital after the business grew. In October, MSCI valued Stripe at approximately $186 billion in the secondary market. A month later, employee offers had already exceeded $200 billion. In the public market, how would investors price a payment company that handles nearly two trillion dollars annually? PayPal provides a good reference point. III. Why is Stripe's $200 Billion Price So Expensive Compared to its Payment Peers? In 2025, Stripe's transaction volume reached $1.9 trillion, while PayPal's total payment volume was $1.79 trillion. The two companies handled roughly the same amount of money annually, with one growing by 34% and the other by 7%. Just looking at the transaction volume, it's clear why buyers are willing to pay Stripe a higher price. Now let's look at revenue. In 2025, Adyen's net revenue was approximately €2.364 billion, a year-on-year increase of 18%; according to media reports, Stripe Group's revenue was approximately $6.8 billion to $6.9 billion, an increase of about one-third. Using these two revenue figures as the denominator, Adyen's market capitalization on November 24th was approximately 11 times its revenue, while Stripe's was approximately 29 times based on a $200 billion valuation. This comparison highlights the difference in group pricing; Stripe's revenue already includes software and other businesses, so 29 times cannot be directly used as its acquiring business multiple. Using Adyen as a reference, we can see how high Stripe's revenue multiple is. To explain the extra $41 billion this year, a more suitable reference is Stripe itself. The buyer in February already offered approximately 23 times net revenue; if net revenue grows by approximately 26% for the whole of 2026, based on the original multiple, it could reach $200 billion. A Business Model Analyst made a projection using the 41% growth rate in the first half of the year. If this pace continues in the second half of the year, based on a valuation of $200 billion, the valuation per dollar of annual net revenue would decrease from approximately $23.4 in the previous round to $20.9. The company's total value is higher, but the offer price per dollar of revenue is lower. This calculation will only be accurate after the full-year revenue and offer price are determined. In fact, simply looking at cold, hard numbers doesn't tell the whole story; the valuation also stems from the current global boom in the AI ​​economy, and what Stripe has already built for this AI economy. IV. Besides Payments, What Else Can Stripe Make Money From? In September in Shanghai, Stripe disclosed that from 2024 to 2025, the number of new AI companies launching on Stripe in Greater China increased by 78%. With new customers coming in, the next question for buyers is: As an AI company grows from its first subscription to multinational operations, which businesses will it gradually entrust to Stripe? A developer launching an AI product in Shanghai might have its first batch of customers from several countries. Customers buy subscriptions and use up their credit in the middle of the month. To complete the task, the backend calls two models with different prices. At the end of the month, the developer needs to both collect payment from customers correctly and know which orders resulted in losses. How much Stripe can earn from this company depends on several things it takes on. The Shanghai exhibition had five columns of display boards, with payments taking up only one. The risk control column provided a ready example: DoorDash uses other payment gateways for some transactions, yet still buys Stripe's Radar to assess risk.

4.1 Pay-as-you-go Billing

An AI company sells monthly subscriptions. A customer uses up their subscription limit and then completes several more tasks. How is the excess usage charged? Is it deducted immediately, or included in the end-of-month bill? These are matters that billing needs to handle. Only after the amount and deduction time are determined can the acquiring department collect the money. In February 2025, Stripe said its billing-centric suite had surpassed $500 million in annualized revenue. A year later, with the addition of Metronome, Stripe set a target of $1 billion in annualized revenue for its entire revenue-generating software suite by 2026. The former figure has already been achieved; the latter remains to be seen by the end of the year, and it involves an additional business segment. Billing also has another layer of value. Payment analyst Dwayne Gefferie points out that OpenAI is also a client of Adyen, and publicly available data doesn't show how many transactions each company processes. However, OpenAI already uses Metronome for billing. Even if a large client outsources some of its acquiring volume, Stripe still has the opportunity to retain billing and software revenue. Competitors have also recognized this opportunity: Adyen acquired Orb, and Salesforce bought m3ter. 4.2 Model Invocation and Token Costs OpenRouter takes Stripe to the other end of the AI ​​merchant spectrum: which model to choose for a single invocation and how many tokens to spend. At the beginning of the year, OpenRouter was Stripe's invoicing and payment customer; by August, Stripe announced its acquisition. Ben Thompson and Lex Sokolin valued the cross-model distribution position; The Information points out that the price discussed at the time was already high relative to expected revenue. The value of this acquisition depends on the gross margin of the router itself and how much billing service these customers will subsequently purchase from Stripe. During a conversation in Shanghai, Kevin Miller, Global Head of Payments at Stripe, likened token expenses to early cloud billing. Having worked at AWS, he witnessed companies initially focusing on getting services running, only to scrutinize the costs of each business line once the bills ballooned. Today's AI applications also suffer from this murky accounting: customers pay one price for one task, while the backend may be adjusting several models. Metronome can credit this revenue to the customer, and OpenRouter has the opportunity to attribute the corresponding model costs back to the same task. Merchants then realize whether their seemingly most popular features are actually profitable. 4.3 Treasury and Merchant Funds Management On Shopify, buyers can pay in USDC, while merchants default to their local currency. Bridge adds options for how money is settled. Let's look at a merchant who has already activated Treasury. After sales proceeds arrive, they can keep them in a Stripe financial account to reserve working capital, remit payments to suppliers, or pay operating expenses through linked cards. For a store, selling goods on Mondays and paying for goods on Fridays are originally two separate transactions. If Stripe can connect these two transactions, a single transaction can potentially generate subsequent currency exchange, payment, and card usage revenue. Parafin addresses another need: when the account balance is insufficient for inventory, the platform can also provide financing to merchants. On the day of the interview in Shanghai, Kevin was out of town and wanted to send an anniversary gift, so he had an agent order flowers for him. For the florist, the order was transferred from their own website to an AI-generated chat window. The florist had to acknowledge the order, and the buyer had to specify how much the agent could spend on their behalf. Stripe handles the catalog and checkout for the florist, while using links and payment tokens to restrict authorization for the buyer. If the florist already uses Stripe for payments, and the same bouquet is ordered through a different payment platform, Stripe is simply retaining the existing business. The additional revenue comes from receiving orders they couldn't get before, or from people willing to pay separately for authorization and risk control. Maintaining this business itself has value. V. Is Stripe still a payment company? When the same bouquet is ordered from a different platform, the florist, the agent, and Stripe each keep their own records for this transaction. Simon Taylor's statement that all AI companies will eventually become payment companies refers precisely to the agent's record. He cited Meta's Muse as an example: today it charges for subscriptions, but in the future, if it facilitates transactions for users, it could potentially take a cut. Taylor was talking about the future. What we can already see today is that many leading AI companies are using Stripe for their business. According to Stripe's August statement to investors, 88% of the companies on the Forbes AI 50 list are using its platform. The letter didn't specify how much of each client's payment volume they were entrusting to Stripe. Not every AI company has the capability, or should be, to build its own payment infrastructure, and Stripe fills that gap. Regardless of the future form of the AI ​​economy, Stripe's largely completed revenue base has already secured its position. In September, in a small bar in Shanghai, we asked Kevin Miller a question. Two months later, seeing the news of this offer negotiation, I remembered it again. Stripe is no longer just a payment company.
